issues.title: Delegated `task` children cannot authenticate HTTP-OAuth MCP servers: `<server>/*` gets 401, explicit refs work only on claude-fable-5.1 and only for some servers

labels.name: area:agents
labels.description: Sub-agents, fleet, autopilot, plan mode, background agents, and custom agents

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server configuration, discovery, connectivity, OAuth, policy, and registry

issues.body:
ustom child agents launched with the native task tool cannot use HTTP-OAuth MCP servers reliably. Two symptoms from the same cause, observed across ~30 delegated runs on 2026-11-10 to 2026-11-12:

1. <server>/* wildcard on an OAuth server → requires authentication in the child. The agent host opens a fresh connection per declared server when a child starts. For HTTP servers it attempts a host-delegated OAuth handoff that never gets a response, falls back to browser OAuth it cannot complete, and sends the request unauthenticated:

The identical three lines are logged for atlassian (https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp). The parent session calls both servers successfully; the stdio testrail server (env-var credentials) works from every child.

2. Explicit <server>/<tool> references behave differently by model and by server. With tools: [..., atlassian/atlassianUserInfo, atlassian/getJiraIssue, ...] (no wildcard): on claude-fable-5.1 the child discovers the tool via tool_search_tool, calls it, and succeeds (7/7 for one agent, 1/1 each for two more profiles). On gpt-6-luna the same agent file discovers the same name and then declines to call it ("no callable invocation interface"), 0/6 attempts — even after instructions explicitly required an attempt. Models were harness defaults; no model override in any failing run. With tools: [..., mabl/get_current_user] on claude-fable-5.1, the child discovers the name and calls it, and the host returns Tool 'mabl-get_current_user' does not exist. So explicit Atlassian refs reach an authorized path that explicit mabl refs do not.

Secondary: tool_search_tool inside a child returns tools not in the child's tools list (e.g. atlassian-executeDestructive, Postman-MCP-*), consistent with #5191.

Affected version:

Agent host copilotVersion 1.0.103-unstable.r41379698026.g3219c66 (from session events), VS Code agent-host client (vscode-agent-host), Windows.

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Configure https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp and https://mcp.mabl.com/mcp (both HTTP OAuth) in .vscode/mcp.json; authorize both in the parent session.
Child A: tools: [read, search, vscode/toolSearch, atlassian/*] → delegate via task, ask it to call atlassianUserInfo once. Observe requires authentication.
Child B: tools: [read, search, vscode/toolSearch, atlassian/atlassianUserInfo], instructions "discover then call exactly once; a name-only discovery result is not evidence it is uncallable". Delegate with model: "claude-fable-5.1" → success. Delegate with default gpt-6-luna → refuses without attempting.
Child C: tools: [read, search, vscode/toolSearch, mabl/get_current_user], model: "claude-fable-5.1" → Tool 'mabl-get_current_user' does not exist after discovery listed it.
Check ~/.copilot/logs/process-*.log for the three-line sequence above for each server at child start.
Expected behavior:

A child inherits the VS Code session's MCP OAuth state for every configured HTTP server (or the host-delegated OAuth handoff succeeds), so <server>/* and <server>/<tool> behave the same from a child as from the parent, independent of model. If children intentionally cannot use OAuth-only HTTP servers, that should be documented so declarations can be designed around it.

Additional context:

Workaround we are using: explicit <server>/<tool> references plus model: "claude-fable-5.1" for Atlassian; for mabl, switching the server to its documented x-api-key header auth (https://help.mabl.com/hc/en-us/articles/48563261741204) so the connection no longer depends on the OAuth handoff. Atlassian's equivalent API-token mode is not enabled for our site, so the model pin remains the only Atlassian path.
Question: is the tool definition actually attached to the model after discovery for explicit refs? Session events record the discovery result but not the per-turn tool list, so we cannot distinguish "model declined an undefined function" from "host did not bind the definition".
No credentials, tenant identifiers, or ticket content included; log lines are redacted as the host prints them.

issues.title: CLI masks structured OpenAI-compatible 403 error message as authentication failure

labels.name: area:models
labels.description: Model selection, availability, switching, rate limits, and model-specific behavior

issues.body:
### Description
When a custom OpenAI-compatible provider returns HTTP 403 with a structured error body, GitHub Copilot CLI reports a generic authentication/provider failure instead of displaying the response's `error.message` and `error.code`.This is misleading for valid 403 responses that are not authentication failures, such as policy or quota decisions. VS Code's Copilot client renders the same response clearly.

### Environment- GitHub Copilot CLI: 1.0.104- OS: Windows- Provider compatibility: OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint

### Minimal synthetic response

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 ForbiddenContent-Type: application/jsonx-ms-error-code: GroupMonthlyTokenQuota
ExceededRetry-After: 86400
{  
"error": {  
"code": "GroupMonthlyTokenQuotaExceeded",  
"type": "insufficient_quota",  
"message": "The monthly token allowance for this group has been exceeded for the current calendar month."  
}}
```

### Actual behavior
Copilot CLI displays a generic provider authentication/API-key failure, such as:

```
textAuthentication failed with provider ... Check your COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY, ...
```

It does not surface the structured `error.message` or `error.code` from the 403 response.

### Suggested handling
Distinguish policy/quota 403 responses from authentication 403 responses by inspecting the structured `error.code` and `error.type`, and render the server-provided message. The `Retry-After` and standard error-code headers can remain available as supplemental context.

### Affected version

1.0.104

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Configure Copilot CLI to use an OpenAI-compatible provider endpoint.
2. Make the endpoint return the response above from a model request.
3. Observe the Copilot CLI message.

### Expected behavior

For a structured OpenAI-compatible 403 response, Copilot CLI should prefer the server-provided error.message and display the error.code, unless the error code/type actually indicates an authentication failure.
Actual authentication errors such as invalid_api_key should retain the existing authentication guidance.

### Additional context

The HTTP status remains intentionally 403; treating this as 429 would be incorrect and could trigger retry loops. A user-agent-specific server workaround would be brittle, so this appears to require client-side presentation logic.

issues.body:
## Problem

On macOS, a keychain prompt keeps appearing for the `copilot-mcp-oauth` service even after choosing "Always Allow":

> security wants to use your confidential information stored in "copilot-mcp-oauth" in your keychain.

The prompt names `security` (`/usr/bin/security`), so the CLI reads the item through the `security` tool.

## Observation

Keychain Access showed about 50 separate `copilot-mcp-oauth` items in the login keychain (kind "application password"), each with a different hashed account name. Their modified dates are spread over every day from 2026-09-30 to the current day, with several created or modified on the same day. The login keychain has no auto-lock timeout (`security show-keychain-info` reports `no-timeout`), so locking does not explain the repeated prompts.

"Always Allow" adds `security` to the access list of one item only. If the CLI creates a new item (or deletes and re-creates it) whenever a token is stored or refreshed, the new item has no grant, and the prompt returns. Old items are also never removed.

## Expected

- Update an existing item in place, so a previous "Always Allow" persists.
- Remove items for tokens that are no longer used.
- Alternatively, store the OAuth tokens for all MCP servers in a single item, so one grant covers them.

## Environment

- Copilot CLI 1.0.99-2, GitHub Copilot app
- macOS, login keychain
- Several remote MCP servers using OAuth (Atlassian, Jama, GitHub)

Related, but a different symptom: #4203

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

`--available-tools` is documented to disable every tool not listed, but an empty value (`--available-tools=` or `--available-tools ''`) sends all 21 built-in tools, the same as omitting the flag. There's no documented way to run `copilot -p` with no tools.


| Flag | Tools sent to the model |
|---|---|
| `--available-tools=` | 21 |
| `--available-tools ''` | 21 |
| `--excluded-tools '*'` | 21 |
| `--available-tools __none__` (a name that matches no tool) | 0 |

The workaround in the last row works, but it relies on unknown tool names being silently ignored.


### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.105

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. In an empty directory, run:
   ```
   copilot -p "Reply with the word ok." -s --model claude-haiku-5.5 \
     --available-tools= --disable-builtin-mcps --no-custom-instructions --no-ask-user
   ```
2. Read the tool count from the newest session's events:
   ```
   EVENTS=$(ls -t ~/.copilot/session-state/*/events.jsonl | head -1)
   jq -rn 'first(inputs | select(.type == "session.usage_checkpoint"))
     | .data.promptCacheBreakState[0].models[]
     | "\(.model): tool_count=\(.tool_count) tool_tokens=\(.tool_tokens)"' "$EVENTS"
   ```
   Output: `claude-haiku-5.5: tool_count=21 tool_tokens=10439`
3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 with `--available-tools __none__`.
   ```
   copilot -p "Reply with the word ok." -s --model claude-haiku-5.5 \
     --available-tools='__none__' --disable-builtin-mcps --no-custom-instructions --no-ask-user
   ```
   Output: `claude-haiku-5.5: tool_count=0 tool_tokens=0`


### Expected behavior

An empty `--available-tools` exposes no tools, or there's a documented way to disable all tools and an empty value is rejected with an error.

### Additional context

For text-only `copilot -p` calls in CI, the unwanted tool definitions add about 10,000 tokens per call. Related: #4596 (system prompt still references removed tools), #407 (list available tools).

issues.title: Windows: launching copilot in a git repo from interactive pwsh kills the parent pwsh.exe (tgrep indexing, 1.0.108)

labels.name: area:platform-windows
labels.description: Windows-specific: PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, WSL, Windows Terminal

labels.name: area:tools
labels.description: Built-in tools: file editing, shell, search, LSP, git, and tool call behavior

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

On Windows, launching `copilot` from an interactive PowerShell 7 session inside a git repository terminates the **parent** `pwsh.exe` with an unhandled exception. The Windows Terminal tab closes, and every process attached to that console goes with it (e.g. an `ssh-agent` started from the shell, so keys have to be re-added).

- Only happens inside a git repository. Outside a git repository, copilot runs normally.
- `USE_TGREP=false` makes it go away, so the trigger appears to be the tgrep indexing that 1.0.108 enabled by default ("enable managed shared tgrep indexing by default for eligible repositories").
- It started today, right after copilot auto-updated to 1.0.108. I have not yet checked whether 1.0.107 is affected.

The crash itself happens in PSReadLine's key-reader thread in the parent shell: while copilot is running, `Console.ReadKey` throws `InvalidOperationException` ("Cannot read keys when either application does not have a console or when console input has been redirected"), and since it is on a background thread with no handler, the whole pwsh process dies. This matches PowerShell/PSReadLine#5197, where console input becomes unavailable for longer than PSReadLine's retry. So something copilot starts for indexing seems to change the state of the console it shares with the parent shell.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.108.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Open a PowerShell 7 tab in Windows Terminal (`pwsh -NoProfile` also reproduces it, so it is not caused by a profile)
2. `cd` into a git repository
3. Run `copilot`
4. Shortly after copilot starts, pwsh.exe crashes and the tab closes

What I checked:

| Variation | Result |
|---|---|
| Outside a git repository | No crash |
| `$env:USE_TGREP = 'false'; copilot` in a git repository | **No crash** |
| `pwsh -NoProfile`, then `copilot` | Crash |
| `Remove-Module PSReadLine`, then `copilot` | Crash (the reader thread is already running, so this does not remove it) |
| Running the real binary directly (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\GitHubCopilotCLI\copilot.exe`) instead of the VS Code `copilot-shim` that comes first on PATH | Crash |
| Git's fsmonitor disabled for copilot (`GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1`, `core.fsmonitor=false`) | Crash (so not caused by `git fsmonitor--daemon`) |

Workaround: `$env:USE_TGREP = 'false'` before launching copilot.

### Expected behavior

copilot and its helper processes (such as the tgrep indexer) should not change the state of the console that the launching shell is using. Starting copilot in a git repository should never terminate the parent shell.

### Additional context

- OS: Windows 11 25H2 (OS Build 26200.9711)
- CPU architecture: <TODO: x86_64 or ARM64>
- Terminal emulator: Windows Terminal
- Shell: PowerShell 7.6.9 (.NET 10.0.14), PSReadLine 2.4.5 (latest on the PowerShell Gallery)

`.NET Runtime` event (Event ID 1026) written when the tab closes:

```
Application: pwsh.exe
CoreCLR Version: 10.0.1426.52326
.NET Version: 10.0.14
Description: The process was terminated due to an unhandled exception.
Exception Info: System.InvalidOperationException: Cannot read keys when either application does not have a console or when console input has been redirected. Try Console.Read.
   at System.ConsolePal.ReadKey(Boolean intercept)
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.Internal.VirtualTerminal._TryIgnoreIOE[T](Func`1 f)
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.Internal.VirtualTerminal.ReadKey()
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.PSConsoleReadLine.ReadOneOrMoreKeys()
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.PSConsoleReadLine.ReadKeyThreadProc()
   at System.Threading.Thread.StartHelper.Callback(Object state)
   at System.Threading.ExecutionContext.RunInternal(ExecutionContext executionContext, ContextCallback callback, Object state)
--- End of stack trace from previous location ---
   at System.Threading.ExecutionContext.RunInternal(ExecutionContext executionContext, ContextCallback callback, Object state)
```

Related: PowerShell/PSReadLine#5197 (on the PSReadLine side, an exhausted retry should not kill the host process). I'm reporting it here as well because the trigger is new in copilot 1.0.108.

issues.title: Agent Plugins 1.0: `.instructions.md` files and `applyTo` frontmatter in `com.github.copilot/rules/` are silently ignored

labels.name: area:context-memory
labels.description: Context window, memory, compaction, checkpoints, and instruction loading

labels.name: area:plugins
labels.description: Plugin system, marketplace, hooks, skills, extensions, and custom agents

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

When packaging a plugin using the **Agent Plugins 1.0.0** format (`"$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/plugin.schema.json"`), Copilot CLI loads skills (`skills/`), MCP servers (`mcp.json`), custom agents (`com.github.copilot/agents/`), hooks (`com.github.copilot/hooks/hooks.json`), and LSP servers (`com.github.copilot/lsp.json`), **but silently ignores standard GitHub Copilot `.instructions.md` files placed in `com.github.copilot/rules/`**.

According to the [CLI plugin reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-plugin-reference#components) and the [VS Code Agent plugin authoring reference](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/reference/agent-plugin-reference), `com.github.copilot/rules/` is the Copilot-specific extension directory for plugin rules/instructions. Across the Copilot ecosystem (`.github/instructions/*.instructions.md`, `~/.copilot/instructions/*.instructions.md`, and VS Code Agent Plugins), the standard Copilot rule format is `*.instructions.md` with YAML frontmatter (`description`, `applyTo`).

Through black-box testing on Copilot CLI `1.0.109`, two cumulative issues prevent `.instructions.md` plugin rules from working across VS Code and Copilot CLI:

1. **`.instructions.md` (and `.md`) files in `com.github.copilot/rules/` are completely ignored.**
   Copilot CLI only discovers files ending in `.mdc` inside `com.github.copilot/rules/`. Files ending in `.instructions.md` or `.md` do not appear in `/env`, `/instructions`, or `copilot instruction list`, are never injected into the prompt, and produce no warning even with `--log-level debug`. Meanwhile, VS Code loads `.instructions.md` from the exact same `com.github.copilot/rules/` folder.
2. **Copilot frontmatter (`applyTo`) is ignored in plugin rules, and `alwaysApply` semantics are inverted for glob-scoped rules.**
   Even after renaming a file from `.instructions.md` to `.mdc`:
   - `applyTo` is ignored; Copilot CLI only parses `globs` (and requires a non-empty `description`), whereas VS Code parses `applyTo` and ignores `globs`.
   - Omitting `alwaysApply` or setting `alwaysApply: false` on a glob-scoped rule (e.g., `globs: ["**/*.yaml"]`) causes `copilot instruction list --json` to report `"defaultDisabled": true` (`0/1 enabled` in `/instructions`). As a result, **glob-scoped rules with `alwaysApply: false` (or omitted) never fire out of the box** when matching files are read unless the user manually enables them in `/instructions` in every session.
   - Counter-intuitively, a rule must set **both** `alwaysApply: true` **and** `globs: [...]` to be enabled by default (`"defaultDisabled": false`) while still scoping activation to matching files rather than injecting globally at startup.


Also, it seems there is another issue with instructions on command like :  **`copilot --plugin-dir <dir> instruction list` ignores `--plugin-dir`.**
   Unlike `copilot --plugin-dir <dir> skill list` (and interactive `/env` / `/instructions`), the `instruction list` subcommand ignores `--plugin-dir` and always prints `No instruction sources found.` unless the plugin is installed into `$COPILOT_HOME`.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.109

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

Run the following self-contained reproduction script in an isolated `COPILOT_HOME`:

```bash
rm -rf /tmp/repro-plugin /tmp/repro-copilot-home
mkdir -p /tmp/repro-plugin/com.github.copilot/rules /tmp/repro-copilot-home

cat << 'EOF' > /tmp/repro-plugin/plugin.json
{
  "$schema": "https://agent-plugins.org/schemas/1.0.0/plugin.schema.json",
  "name": "repro-plugin",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Minimal reproducer for plugin instructions"
}
EOF

# 1. Standard Copilot .instructions.md file -> SILENTLY IGNORED
cat << 'EOF' > /tmp/repro-plugin/com.github.copilot/rules/standard-copilot.instructions.md
---
name: "Standard Copilot Rule"
description: "Standard Copilot instruction file using applyTo"
applyTo: "**/*.yaml"
---
Follow standard YAML conventions.
EOF

# 2. .mdc with globs and alwaysApply: false -> DISCOVERED, BUT DISABLED BY DEFAULT
cat << 'EOF' > /tmp/repro-plugin/com.github.copilot/rules/mdc-glob-disabled.mdc
---
description: "MDC rule with globs and alwaysApply false"
globs: ["**/*.yaml"]
alwaysApply: false
---
Follow MDC YAML conventions (disabled by default).
EOF

# 3. .mdc with globs and alwaysApply: true -> ENABLED BY DEFAULT & SCOPED TO GLOBS
cat << 'EOF' > /tmp/repro-plugin/com.github.copilot/rules/mdc-glob-enabled.mdc
---
description: "MDC rule with globs and alwaysApply true"
globs: ["**/*.yaml"]
alwaysApply: true
---
Follow MDC YAML conventions (enabled).
EOF
```

#### Step A — Test `instruction list` with `--plugin-dir` (Bug 4)

```bash
COPILOT_HOME=/tmp/repro-copilot-home copilot --plugin-dir /tmp/repro-plugin instruction list
```

Actual output:
```text
No instruction sources found.
```
*(Whereas launching interactively with `copilot --plugin-dir /tmp/repro-plugin` and running `/env` or `/instructions` **does** find the `.mdc` files, and `copilot --plugin-dir <dir> skill list` honors `--plugin-dir`.)*

#### Step B — Install the plugin and inspect `copilot instruction list --json` (Bugs 1 & 2)

```bash
COPILOT_HOME=/tmp/repro-copilot-home copilot plugin install /tmp/repro-plugin
COPILOT_HOME=/tmp/repro-copilot-home copilot instruction list --json
```

Actual output:
```json
[
  {
    "id": "plugin-rule/repro-plugin:mdc-glob-disabled",
    "label": "repro-plugin: mdc-glob-disabled",
    "description": "MDC rule with globs and alwaysApply false",
    "location": "plugin",
    "type": "plugin",
    "sourcePath": "/tmp/repro-copilot-home/installed-plugins/_direct/repro-plugin-xxxx/com.github.copilot/rules/mdc-glob-disabled.mdc",
    "defaultDisabled": true,
    "applyTo": [
      "**/*.yaml"
    ]
  },
  {
    "id": "plugin-rule/repro-plugin:mdc-glob-enabled",
    "label": "repro-plugin: mdc-glob-enabled",
    "description": "MDC rule with globs and alwaysApply true",
    "location": "plugin",
    "type": "plugin",
    "sourcePath": "/tmp/repro-copilot-home/installed-plugins/_direct/repro-plugin-xxxx/com.github.copilot/rules/mdc-glob-enabled.mdc",
    "defaultDisabled": false,
    "applyTo": [
      "**/*.yaml"
    ]
  }
]
```

Notice that:
- `standard-copilot.instructions.md` is completely missing from the discovered sources.
- `mdc-glob-disabled.mdc` has `"defaultDisabled": true`, so in a session (`/instructions`) it starts unchecked (`•`) and does not trigger when reading a `.yaml` file.
- `mdc-glob-enabled.mdc` has `"defaultDisabled": false` and `"applyTo": ["**/*.yaml"]` (mapped from `globs`, while an actual `applyTo` key in frontmatter is ignored).

### Summary of observed behavior matrix

| File in `com.github.copilot/rules/` | Frontmatter | VS Code behavior | Copilot CLI `1.0.109` behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rule.instructions.md` | `description` + `applyTo: "**"` | Loaded (global) | **Silently ignored** |
| `rule.instructions.md` | `description` + `applyTo: "**/*.yaml"` | Loaded (glob-scoped) | **Silently ignored** |
| `rule.mdc` | `description` + `applyTo: "**/*.yaml"` | Loaded (glob-scoped) | Discovered, **`applyTo` ignored**, disabled by default (`defaultDisabled: true`) |
| `rule.mdc` | `description` + `globs: ["**/*.yaml"]` + `alwaysApply: false` (or omitted) | Loaded, **`globs` ignored** | Discovered, **disabled by default** (`0/1 enabled` in `/instructions`; never triggers unless manually toggled per session) |

### Expected behavior

1. **Support `.instructions.md` natively in `com.github.copilot/rules/`**: Since `com.github.copilot/` is GitHub Copilot's own client extension namespace in Agent Plugins 1.0, Copilot CLI should discover `*.instructions.md` files alongside `*.mdc` (matching `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md`, `~/.copilot/instructions/*.instructions.md`, and VS Code's plugin loader).
2. **Support Copilot frontmatter (`applyTo`) and intuitive activation defaults**:
   - Accept `applyTo` (string or array) in addition to `globs` so a single `.instructions.md` file works identically in both VS Code and Copilot CLI without duplicating metadata.
   - Treat glob-scoped rules (`applyTo` / `globs` without `alwaysApply: false`) as enabled for pattern-matching by default, rather than disabled for the whole session unless `alwaysApply: true` is also set. When `applyTo` is `"**"` or `"*"`, treat the rule as session-wide.
3. **Honor `--plugin-dir` in `copilot instruction list`**: Match `copilot skill list` and interactive sessions so plugin authors can validate `com.github.copilot/rules/` during local development without reinstalling the plugin on every edit.
4. **Document the `com.github.copilot/rules/` file format and frontmatter contract** in the [CLI plugin reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-plugin-reference#components).

### Additional context

- **OS:** Linux (`x86_64`, Ubuntu / WSL2)
- **Shell:** `bash`
- **Impact & current workaround:** As VS Code deprecates its legacy Local harness in favor of the shared Copilot harness, organizations migrating shared engineering harnesses to **Agent Plugins 1.0** need a single plugin package to deliver skills, MCP servers, agents, hooks, LSPs, and `.instructions.md` rules across both VS Code and Copilot CLI. Currently, the only way to avoid duplicating every rule file in `com.github.copilot/rules/` is to include both `applyTo` and `globs` + `alwaysApply: true` in each `.instructions.md` frontmatter and commit relative `<name>.mdc -> <name>.instructions.md` symlinks alongside them (which breaks on Windows checkouts when `core.symlinks=false`).

issues.title: Regression: sandboxed git has no way to use a credential that differs from the Copilot/gh sign-in identity

labels.name: area:permissions
labels.description: Tool approval, security boundaries, sandbox mode, and directory restrictions

labels.name: area:tools
labels.description: Built-in tools: file editing, shell, search, LSP, git, and tool call behavior

issues.body:
### Summary

`sandbox.auth.git` authenticates sandboxed git using only the Copilot/gh sign-in identity. There's no way to supply a different credential (e.g. fine-grained PAT). The sandbox injects an empty, highest-precedence `credential.helper` override into every sandboxed git subprocess, discarding any helper configured in `.git/config`. This is independent of `auth.git`/`auth.gh` settings.

Related tickets #4804 #1460 

### Regression marker

 v1.0.92  (2026-10-05) changelog: "Sandboxed scripts that run Git now authenticate with masked credentials and SSH remote rewrites."  v1.0.91  does not exhibit this.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.92

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

```bash
mkdir repo && cd repo && git init
cat > /tmp/fake-helper.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
echo "username=alice"
echo "password=hunter2"
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/fake-helper.sh
git config --local credential.helper '!/tmp/fake-helper.sh'

# Works on the host:
printf 'protocol=https\nhost=example.com\n\n' | git credential fill
# -> username=alice / password=hunter2

# Fails identically inside the sandbox:
copilot --sandbox --add-dir . -p "printf 'protocol=https\nhost=example.com\n\n' | git credential fill"
```

Host: helper fills the fake credential correctly.
Sandboxed: `bash
git config --show-origin --show-scope --get-all credential.helper
` shows the local helper present, but a trailing  command line: scope entry with an empty value overrides it ( env | grep GIT_CONFIG  shows  GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=6 ,  GIT_CONFIG_KEY_5=credential.helper ,  GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_5=  empty).  git credential fill  returns nothing; real-world  git clone / pull  against a credential-helper-only remote fails with  `fatal: unable to get password from user` .

### Expected behavior

Sandboxed git should have a supported way to authenticate as an identity other than whichever account Copilot itself is signed in as :

- Let the masking process accept a user-supplied credential.
Extend `sandbox.auth.git` (or `sandbox.credentials.envVars`) to accept a PAT/token supplied by the user (e.g. via a settings field or an env var name to mask), and have the masking proxy substitute that credential into git's HTTPS requests instead of always deriving it from the Copilot/gh sign-in session. This would let native masking work for repos/orgs the signed-in identity can't access, without exposing the raw token to the sandboxed process.

- Don't force out a user-configured `credential.helper` when native masking isn't handling that credential.
Today, the sandbox always injects an empty, highest-precedence `credential.helper` override into every sandboxed git subprocess, regardless of `auth.git`/`auth.gh`. This unconditionally discards any helper a user configured in `.git/config`, even when `auth.git` is off and no native masking is in play for that request. Could be opt-in/configurable, e.g. a sandbox policy flag (`sandbox.auth.gitCredentialHelper` or similar) that leaves a user-configured helper intact when native git masking isn't being used for that repo/host, so a custom helper can still supply credentials for identities the built-in masking doesn't cover.

issues.title: macOS local sandbox: expose an exact Mach/XPC lookup allowlist

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

GitHub Copilot CLI's macOS local sandbox does not expose a way to allow a specific third-party Mach/XPC service.

A concrete example is 1Password CLI desktop app integration, which needs to look up:

```text
2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password.browser-helper
```

This blocks credential-helper chains such as:

```text
aws
  -> credential_process
     -> credential helper script
        -> op CLI
           -> NSXPCConnection / mach-lookup
              -> 2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password.browser-helper
```

Granting access to the executables, configuration files, 1Password Unix socket, and network destinations is not enough. Seatbelt treats Mach service discovery as the separate `mach-lookup` capability.

Copilot CLI `1.0.86-0` exposes only `keychainAccess` under `sandbox.userPolicy.seatbelt`. Its installed API schema defines `SandboxConfigUserPolicySeatbelt` with only that property and `additionalProperties: false`. Adding `extraMachLookups` to user settings produces no validation error, but the setting is inert and does not change the effective Seatbelt policy.

`keychainAccess` is not a substitute for an XPC allowlist. It grants a broad set of Apple Keychain and trust services plus Keychain-related filesystem paths, but it does not allow the third-party 1Password browser-helper service. The remaining workaround is to bypass the sandbox for the command, removing substantially more isolation than this workflow requires.

The underlying Microsoft MXC Seatbelt backend already supports exact-name lookups through `seatbelt.extraMachLookups`. The missing layer appears to be Copilot CLI's settings/API pass-through to MXC rather than a macOS Seatbelt limitation.

### Proposed solution

Expose MXC's exact-name Mach lookup list in Copilot's sandbox policy:

```json
{
  "sandbox": {
    "userPolicy": {
      "seatbelt": {
        "extraMachLookups": [
          "2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password.browser-helper"
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The minimum implementation could pass each configured value to MXC's existing `seatbelt.extraMachLookups` field, producing a narrow rule equivalent to:

```scheme
(allow mach-lookup
  (global-name "2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password.browser-helper"))
```

Suggested security properties and acceptance criteria:

- Accept exact Mach service names only. Reject empty values, glob patterns, regular expressions, and prefix wildcards.
- Keep the setting independent from `keychainAccess`.
- Include the effective lookup list in `/sandbox policy` so the grant is visible and auditable.
- Confirm that the configured 1Password helper lookup succeeds while an unrelated Mach service remains denied.
- Do not implicitly grant `mach-register`, all Mach lookups, GUI access, Apple Events, or a raw Seatbelt profile override.

### Example prompts or workflows

With an AWS profile whose `credential_process` refreshes through 1Password desktop integration:

> List the caller identity for this AWS profile.

The AWS CLI invokes its credential helper, which invokes `op`. The helper should reach the configured 1Password XPC service without the entire command running outside the sandbox.

### Additional context

Environment:

- GitHub Copilot CLI `1.0.86-0`
- macOS `26.6.2` (`25G83`)
- Apple silicon (`arm64`)
- 1Password CLI `2.38.1`

To isolate the blocked capability from credentials and the rest of the AWS helper chain, I compiled a small probe whose only relevant operation is:

```c
bootstrap_look_up(
  bootstrap_port,
  "2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password.browser-helper",
  &port
);
```

The probe does not call `op`, retrieve a credential, access a Unix socket, or make a network request. I ran the identical binary in each context:

| Context | Copilot Seatbelt setting | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Host, outside Copilot's sandbox | Not applicable | Exit `0`: `mach-lookup allowed` |
| Copilot Bash tool in the local sandbox | `keychainAccess: true` | Exit `1`: `mach-lookup failed: 1100 (Permission denied)` |
| Copilot Bash tool using an isolated settings directory | Proposed `extraMachLookups` value | Exit `1`: `mach-lookup failed: 1100 (Permission denied)` |

The host result confirms that the service is registered. The sandbox result isolates the failure to `mach-lookup`; unrelated socket, filesystem, network, and Keychain grants cannot satisfy that operation. The isolated-settings result confirms that `extraMachLookups` is silently ineffective in Copilot `1.0.86-0`.

This diagnostic does not reproduce the full credential chain. A sandboxed AWS command can succeed while credentials are cached; the user-visible failure occurs when the helper must refresh through 1Password desktop integration.

Relevant references:

- [MXC macOS Seatbelt backend](https://github.com/microsoft/mxc/blob/main/docs/seatbelt/seatbelt-backend.md#seatbelt-specific-options) documents `extraMachLookups` as exact service names and describes the broader `keychainAccess` and `guiAccess` grants.
- [anthropics/sandbox-runtime#83](https://github.com/anthropics/sandbox-runtime/issues/83) reported the same 1Password XPC limitation; Anthropic subsequently exposed `allowMachLookup`.
- [microsoft/mxc#887](https://github.com/microsoft/mxc/issues/887) tracks exposure of backend-specific configuration through shared SDK layers.
- [Copilot CLI sandbox configuration documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/cloud-and-local-sandboxes/configuring-local-sandbox-settings) documents Keychain support but no narrow third-party Mach/XPC allowlist.

issues.title: Local sandbox 'Authenticate gh' silently uses an unrelated cached fine-grained PAT instead of active gh OAuth session, with no visibility into which credential is chosen
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

With local sandboxing enabled (`/sandbox enable`) and the "Authenticate gh" auth setting on (default), the `GH_TOKEN` exported into the sandboxed environment did not correspond to my active `gh` session.

- `gh auth status` (run on the host, outside the sandbox) showed I was logged in via the OAuth device flow, with a `gho_...` token and scopes `admin:public_key`, `gist`, `read:org`, `repo` — i.e. full private repo access.
- Inside a Copilot CLI sandboxed session, `echo $GH_TOKEN` / `gh repo list <org> --visibility private` showed access to only **one** private repository in my org, via a token in the fine-grained PAT format (`github_pat_...`).
- After investigating, I found the actual token being used: an old fine-grained PAT I had created previously and scoped intentionally to a single, unrelated repository (not the repo I was actively working in).
- This PAT is neither the active `gh auth status` OAuth session (keyring-stored `gho_` token) nor the GitHub App `ghu_` token found in `~/.config/github-copilot/auth.db`.

I was unable to determine, from inside a Copilot CLI session or from documentation, **why this specific cached PAT was selected** over my active OAuth login, or where exactly it was being read from/cached. The lack of visibility made this very difficult to diagnose — I only found the answer by manually checking GitHub's "Active tokens" org admin page and recognizing a token I had created weeks earlier for unrelated purposes.

### Expected behavior

When "Authenticate gh" is enabled for the local sandbox, I would expect one of the following:
1. The sandbox's `GH_TOKEN` to be derived from the currently active `gh auth status` account/session (respecting `gh auth switch`), not from some other cached credential, OR
2. If Copilot CLI intentionally uses a different/cached credential for the sandbox (e.g. a previously-supplied `GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN` env var), this should be clearly surfaced to the user — e.g. via `/sandbox` or `/env`, showing *which* token/account is being exported into the sandbox and why, without requiring the user to manually diff PAT prefixes and check GitHub's org "Active tokens" page.

### Reproduction steps

1. Log in normally via `gh auth login` (OAuth device flow), confirm with `gh auth status` that the active session has broad `repo` scope.
2. Separately, at some earlier point, create (or have previously created) a fine-grained PAT scoped to only one specific repository, for an unrelated purpose.
3. Launch `copilot`, enable local sandboxing (`/experimental on` if needed, then `/sandbox enable`), leave "Authenticate gh" at its default (on).
4. Inside the Copilot CLI session, ask the agent to run `gh repo list <org> --visibility private` or inspect `$GH_TOKEN`.
5. Observe that the token exported into the sandbox matches the old, narrowly-scoped fine-grained PAT from step 2 — not the active OAuth session from step 1 — with no indication in the CLI of which credential was selected or why.

### Additional context

- `/env` and `/sandbox` do not currently surface which specific token/account was selected for `GH_TOKEN` in the sandbox, making this essentially undiagnosable without manual, external investigation (comparing token prefixes, checking org "Active tokens" pages, etc.).
- Docs reference (`Configuring local sandbox settings` → Auth tab): "Authenticate gh: Export GH_TOKEN so that GitHub CLI ... works inside the sandbox without reaching its stored credentials (configuration directory or OS keychain), which the sandbox blocks." This explains *that* a substitute token is exported, but not how that substitute is selected when multiple credentials (OAuth session, GitHub App ghu_ token, cached fine-grained PATs) exist on the host.
- Related open issues that touch on adjacent auth-scoping concerns: #1460 (no scoped-auth workflow vs `gh auth login`), #953 (default OAuth grants excessive scope).

### Suggested improvement

- Add a way to inspect, from within a session (e.g. `/sandbox` Auth tab or `/env`), exactly which token/account is currently selected for sandboxed `gh`/git operations, including its origin (active `gh auth status` session vs. a manually-set `GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN` env var vs. some other cached credential) and its repository scope.
- Consider making the sandboxed `GH_TOKEN` follow the currently active `gh auth status` account by default, rather than silently preferring a possibly-stale `GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN` env var or other cached credential.

issues.title: macOS sandbox:  allowLocalNetwork: true  still generates  hostLoopback: deny  in proxy mode, blocking Gradle on CLI 1.0.107

labels.name: area:permissions
labels.description: Tool approval, security boundaries, sandbox mode, and directory restrictions

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

## Summary

Gradle fails inside the Copilot CLI macOS sandbox because its client cannot connect to its localhost daemon, despite the configuration explicitly enabling outbound and local networking.

The daemon starts successfully and listens on  `127.0.0.1`. However, the generated policy for the failing command contains:

```json
{
  "network": {
    "egress": {
      "default": "deny"
    },
    "ingress": {
      "default": "allow",
      "hostLoopback": "deny"
    },
    "runtimeConfig": {
      "networkProxy": "http://127.0.0.1:57901"
    }
  }
}
```

The Gradle daemon in that run listened on port  57903 , not the permitted proxy port  57901 .

An independent socket probe also confirmed that binding and listening on localhost succeeds, while connecting to that listener fails with  EPERM .

This appears to be a persistence or regression of #5105, which is currently closed.

## Environment

- GitHub Copilot CLI: 1.0.107
 - macOS: 26.7.1
 - Architecture: arm64
 - Gradle wrapper: 9.8.2
 - Java: Eclipse Temurin 25.0.1

The project is a small standalone Java application using Gradle’s application plugin.

## Relevant configuration

The following is a sanitized excerpt. An additional private artifact-registry hostname and unrelated settings have been omitted.

```json
{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "allowBypass": true,
    "allowDevToolAccess": true,
    "addCurrentWorkingDirectory": true,
    "auth": {
      "git": true,
      "gh": true
    },
    "userPolicy": {
      "network": {
        "allowOutbound": true,
        "allowLocalNetwork": true,
        "allowedHosts": [
          "127.0.0.1",
          "services.gradle.org"
        ],
        "blockedHosts": []
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Additional filesystem grants provide read/write access to the Gradle user home and read access to the JDK/toolchain locations. The user-level filesystem deny list is empty.

## Steps to reproduce

1. On macOS, use Copilot CLI  1.0.107  with sandboxing enabled.
2. Enable outbound and local networking, with a non-empty host allowlist that includes  127.0.0.1 . Git and GitHub CLI credential masking are also enabled in this reproduction.
3. Open a Java project using the Gradle  9.8.2  wrapper and Temurin Java  25.0.1 .
4. Ask Copilot to execute:
./gradlew build --debug --no-daemon
5. Inspect the debug output and the generated command policy under:
~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/policies/

## Expected behavior

With  allowLocalNetwork: true , sandboxed commands should be able to make direct TCP connections to localhost, including to build daemons they start themselves, subject to any explicitly enforced managed restrictions.

A deny-by-default egress policy is understandable when a proxy enforces the remote host allowlist. However, the requested loopback permission should be represented by an appropriate loopback exception.

If local networking intentionally means only proxy-mediated HTTP access, the documentation and settings UI should clearly distinguish that from direct localhost TCP access.

## Actual behavior and diagnostic evidence

The daemon starts successfully

Gradle reports:

> Successfully started process 'Gradle build daemon'

The daemon log confirms that it is listening on:

> 127.0.0.1:57903

The client then attempts that connection and immediately reports:

> Trying to connect to address /127.0.0.1.
> Cannot connect to address /127.0.0.1, skipping.

The command exits with code `1`:

> Could not connect to the Gradle daemon.
>
> No build tasks execute.

The effective policy denies host loopback

The policy corresponding to the debug build contains:

```json
"ingress": {
  "default": "allow",
  "hostLoopback": "deny"
}
```

Its proxy endpoint is `http://127.0.0.1:57901`.

This is consistent with allowing listeners and access to the proxy, while denying direct connections to other localhost ports. Adding  `127.0.0.1` to `allowedHosts` does not remove this effective denial.

A standalone socket probe reproduces the denial

A Python probe created a TCP listener on an ephemeral IPv4 loopback port and attempted to connect to it from the same process:

> Loopback bind/listen succeeded: 127.0.0.1:57947
> Loopback connect failed: PermissionError, errno=1, Operation not permitted

This isolates the failure from Gradle, dependency resolution, and external networking.

Proxy variables are injected

A subsequent sandboxed command received all uppercase and lowercase forms of `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ALL_PROXY`, pointing to a local proxy. `NO_PROXY` and `no_proxy` were unset.

Gradle’s daemon connection uses direct TCP, not HTTP, so these proxy variables cannot carry the daemon protocol.

`--no-daemon` does not avoid the connection

Gradle still launches a single-use daemon because the wrapper JVM does not satisfy the build’s JVM requirements. The debug output identifies insufficient maximum heap size; the wrapper starts with `-Xmx64m`.

These commands all failed with the daemon connection error:

```
./gradlew build
./gradlew build --no-daemon -Dorg.gradle.jvmargs=
./gradlew build --debug --no-daemon
```

Requested investigation

Please check how `sandbox.userPolicy.network.allowLocalNetwork` maps to MXC’s `network.ingress.hostLoopback` when proxy enforcement is active.

In this reproduction, local networking is requested, but the generated policy still sets `hostLoopback: "deny"`. Please clarify whether this is a policy-generation defect, a managed-policy override, or an intentional restriction.

If intentional, please document a supported way to permit build-daemon loopback connections without disabling the sandbox or removing remote host filtering.

_No response_

issues.title: Windows: Entra broker token cache stays 0 bytes after MCP sign-in, so every new process re-prompts

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

After I sign in through the Microsoft Entra account broker for an HTTP MCP server, the token cache file stays empty. Every new process shows the account picker again. A `/restart` in the same process does not prompt.

`~\.copilot\entra-broker-accounts\<id>.bin` is written (1,974 bytes) when I pick the account. `~\.copilot\entra-broker-cache\<id>.bin` stays at 0 bytes. I did not read the file contents.

### Affected version

1.0.103

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Add an HTTP MCP server that uses Entra sign-in to `~\.copilot\mcp-config.json`: `{"mcpServers": {"EngHub": {"type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.eng.ms", "tools": ["*"]}}}`
2. Start a session. The CLI shows `Authenticating: EngHub` and the Windows "Pick an account" dialog.
3. Pick the signed-in account. Authentication succeeds.
4. Check the file sizes in `~\.copilot\entra-broker-cache\` and `~\.copilot\entra-broker-accounts\`. The cache file is 0 bytes.
5. Exit and start a new session. The account picker shows again.
6. Run `/restart` in a running session. No prompt shows.

### Expected behavior

The token is saved in `entra-broker-cache`. A new process signs in silently without the account picker.

### Additional context

- OS: Windows, x64
- Shell: PowerShell
- Launched with `agency copilot` (Agency 2026.10.20.6)
- I deleted the empty cache file and signed in again. It was recreated at 0 bytes.
- Related but different: #4464 (repeated interactive sign-in from refresh scope errors), #5068 and #5088 (Windows account broker failures).

issues.title: --no-alt-screen was silently removed with no replacement — alt-screen is now unavoidable and broken

labels.name: area:terminal-rendering
labels.description: Display and rendering: flickering, scrolling, line wrapping, output formatting

issues.body:
Alt-screen/fullscreen mode is a genuine regression for a lot of us, and it's
been reported since March (#1799, #2334) with no resolution.

What makes this worse: the `--no-alt-screen` flag that used to let people
opt out has now been removed entirely, with no deprecation notice and no
replacement setting. Running it now just fails:

    $ copilot --no-alt-screen
    error: unknown option '--no-alt-screen'

I checked `/settings` for an equivalent key and found nothing that restores
inline/streaming rendering. So as of the current release, there is no
supported way to turn off fullscreen mode at all.

This isn't a nice-to-have. Alt-screen breaks:
- native terminal scrollback (can't scroll up past the current screen)
- terminal search (Cmd+F / Ctrl+F can't see history)
- copy/paste in some terminal emulators
- usability in tmux/screen and browser-based terminals

Please either:
1. Restore `--no-alt-screen` (or an equivalent `/settings` key), or
2. Clearly document the replacement if one exists and I'm missing it.

Removing an escape hatch that people were actively relying on, without
warning, is a bad pattern. At minimum this needs a documented workaround.

issues.title: [Feature request] Add setting to disable agent checkpoint refs (refs/agents/*)

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

Every agent turn creates a commit under `refs/agents/<session-id>/checkpoints/turn/N` in the user's repository. These refs: - are authored with the user's own git identity (user.name/user.email) - appear in any tool that renders all refs (e.g. GitLens Commit Graph),   burying the user's actual history under dozens of "Agent host session" rows - cannot be disabled via any exposed setting - checkpoints are created even for read-only turns, which makes the noise-to-value ratio worst exactly for users who never let the agent write.

### Proposed solution

A configuration option (e.g. `agent.checkpoints.enabled: false`) to disable
git-ref checkpointing entirely, or alternatively:

### Bug

Copilot CLI 1.0.109 loses a multiline paste when Enter arrives during startup while managed-account policy is still loading. The composer retains `[Paste #1 - N lines]`, but the pasted body is discarded; a later submission produces an empty user message.

### Reproduction

1. Launch the interactive Copilot CLI with a policy load taking longer than about 0.6 seconds.
2. Immediately paste a multiline prompt and press Enter about 0.6 seconds after launch.
3. Observe `Managed account policy is still loading. Please wait a moment and try again.` Press Enter after the policy resolves and inspect the submitted message.

### Actual

The placeholder remains in the composer, but the submitted user message has empty content. In observed failures the policy warning appeared at +0.60-0.66 seconds; policy resolved at +1.09-1.17 seconds. The same 95-line text failed once and worked on retry, so length was not the cause.

### Expected

Queue submission until policy readiness, or retain the pasted body when submission is rejected so it can be retried without losing text.

Related: #218 reports a different form of input loss.

issues.title: Quoted strings that happen to start with / are misinterpreted as paths the agent intends to read or write

labels.name: area:permissions

labels.name: area:tools
labels.description: Built-in tools: file editing, shell, search, LSP, git, and tool call behavior

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

## Description

The GitHub Copilot CLI's path-access scanner misclassifies quoted shell-command arguments that happen to start with `/` as filesystem paths the action intends to read or write, even when the receiving command is a no-op or treats the argument as literal data.

The scanner inspects bash-tool command text before execution. In the tested forms, a quoted argument whose first character is `/` triggers an interactive "Allow directory access" permission prompt, presenting the argument as a candidate directory the action may read or write.

The trigger appears to depend on the token's leading character (a forward slash) rather than on whether the receiving command opens the token as a filesystem path, and rather than on whether the token names an existing directory. Strings such as `/))` (which does not name an existing directory and is not accessed by the receiving command) and `/tmp is a sentence` (whose `/tmp` prefix is allowlisted in the bare unquoted form but is not protected once the quoted argument is extended with non-path characters) both trigger the prompt.

The scanner appears to treat `echo` and the tested `awk` program-argument form differently from other tested commands: those pass, while most other tested commands trigger the prompt, including no-ops such as `true` and `:`, and data-only commands such as `printf`.

This is closely related to https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/774, which describes a similar lexical-scanning failure mode rejecting command-like words in text arguments passed to non-bash tools. The present report covers a complementary case within the bash-tool path: arguments are scanned by token shape rather than by whether the receiving command would actually open them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Invoke one of the tested non-exempt commands, such as `true`, `:`, or `printf`, with a quoted argument whose first character is a forward slash (`/`). In the tested cases, the remainder of the string varied widely — from an allowlisted-prefix extension like `/tmp is a sentence`, to a path-shaped sensitive substring like `/etc/passwd`, to a string that does not name any directory in the tested environment like `/))` — and the prompt fired in every case.
2. The string need not be a valid path; it need not exist on disk; the command need not access files.
3. The scanner intercepts the call before bash runs with an "Allow directory access" permission prompt that defaults to "Yes, and add these directories to the allowed list".

## Example

### Quoted string starting with `/` passed to `true`

```bash
true '/))'
```

The CLI displays this interactive prompt before executing:

```
╭─ Allow directory access ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
│                                                                  │
│ This action may read or write the following path outside your    │
│ allowed directory list.                                          │
│                                                                  │
│ ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │
│ │ /))                                                          │ │
│ ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ │
│                                                                  │
│ Do you want to allow this?                                       │
│                                                                  │
│   1. Yes                                                         │
│ ❯ 2. Yes, and add these directories to the allowed list          │
│   3. No (Esc)                                                    │
│                                                                  │
│ ↑↓ to navigate · Enter to select · Esc to cancel                 │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

`true` is the universal POSIX no-op: it ignores every argument and returns success. The argument `/))` does not name an existing directory in the tested environment, is not sensitive-looking, and is not accessed by `true` — it is simply a string that happens to start with `/`. Yet the prompt's title — "Allow directory access" — and the candidate text shown in its own bordered box indicate the CLI is treating `/))` as a filesystem path the action may read or write. The default option ("Yes, and add these directories to the allowed list") would proceed with the call; based on that option's label, I would expect accepting it to also persist `/))` in the allowed-directory list.

### Quoted argument that begins with an allowlisted bare token (`/tmp`)

```bash
true '/tmp is a sentence'
```

Same prompt, with `/tmp is a sentence` shown as the candidate directory. This is striking because the unquoted variant `true /tmp` passes (see Contrast table below): the allowlist that protects `/tmp` does not carry through to a quoted argument whose first character is `/`, even when the quoted content starts with the same allowlisted prefix.

### Quoted path-shaped string passed to the null builtin

```bash
: '/tmp is a noop arg'
```

Same prompt, with `/tmp is a noop arg` shown as the candidate directory. `:` is the shell null command and never inspects its arguments.

### Argument to printf

```bash
printf '%s\n' '/tmp is a noop arg'
```

Same prompt, with the quoted argument shown as the candidate directory. `printf` treats this argument as data substituted into the format string, not as a path to read. A separately tested format-string case, `printf '/tmp is a noop arg\n'`, also triggers the same prompt, so the observed scan is not limited to printf's data arguments; both tested positions are subject to it.

### `command` builtin does not change the outcome

```bash
command true '/tmp is a sentence'
```

Same prompt, with the quoted argument shown as the candidate directory. Wrapping the command with the `command` builtin does not change the scanner's classification.

### Contrast: tested forms that the scanner passes

| Form | Result |
|---|---|
| `echo '/etc/passwd is a sentence'` | passes |
| `echo /etc/passwd` (unquoted) | passes |
| `echo '/var/log was the locus'` | passes |
| `awk '/error/ {print}'` (the awk regex starts with `/`) | passes |
| `true /foo` | passes |
| `true /tmp` | passes |
| `true /xyz` | passes |

The scanner clearly recognizes single-quoting (it extracts the full quoted content as a single candidate path) and appears to treat `echo` and the tested `awk` form differently from other commands: `echo` arguments pass in both quoted and unquoted forms, and the tested `awk` program-argument form passes even when its first character is `/`. Comparable arguments to `true`, `:`, and `printf` trigger the permission prompt. Additionally, the tested forms `true /foo`, `true /tmp`, and `true /xyz` pass even though the receiving command is `true` — which does trigger the prompt for other tested arguments. What is not modeled in the tested forms is the receiving command's semantics: `true`, `:`, and `printf` never open files at the named path in the tested forms, yet their arguments are still subject to the path-access rule. Conversely, a quoted argument whose first character is not `/` does not trigger the prompt even when `/` appears later in the token: `true '(/ 10 2)'` passes, supporting the inference that the trigger condition is the token's leading character rather than the presence of `/` anywhere in the token.

### Asymmetry: commands that pass vs. `true`

`echo '/etc/passwd is a sentence'` passes but `true '/etc/passwd is a sentence'` triggers the permission prompt. Similarly, `awk '/error/ {print}'` passes — the awk regex argument's leading `/` is not flagged — but the same content passed to `true` (`true '/error/ {print}'`) does trigger the permission prompt. The tested commands have the same filesystem-access semantics with respect to these arguments: none of them opens the argument as a file. The asymmetry suggests command-specific treatment for `echo` and the tested `awk` form rather than a general rule about whether the argument can be opened as a path.

I have not exhaustively tested every command, every leading-`/` argument shape, every allowlisted path, or every argument position. The claims here are limited to the tested contrast cases above and to the reproducible permission prompts.

## Expected Behavior

A semantics-aware path-access guard would:

* Distinguish between commands that use arguments as filesystem paths (e.g., `cat`, `mv`, `cp`, `chmod`) and commands that do not open the tested argument positions as paths (e.g., `true`, `:`, `printf`, and `echo`).
* Apply the path-access rule only to arguments at positions where the receiving command will treat the argument as a filesystem path.
* Treat literal text data passed to data-only commands as data, not as path-access claims.

## Actual Behavior

The observed behavior is consistent with the scanner inspecting quoted leading-`/` arguments for the tested non-exempt commands and treating them as candidate directory-access strings without distinguishing:

* Whether the receiving command opens arguments as filesystem paths.
* Whether any argument position of the receiving command can open filesystem paths; in the tested `printf` cases, both format-string and data positions are scanned even though neither is opened as a path.
* Whether the bytes name an existing directory or just happen to have a leading `/`.

Within the tested forms, the scanner appears to recognize quoting (it extracts the entire quoted content as a single candidate path) and to pass arguments to `echo` and the tested `awk` form, but it does not pass comparable arguments to other tested commands or argument positions.

## Impact

* **Requires interactive approval for string operations that do not access files**: print operations such as `printf '%s' '/tmp is a noop arg'` trigger the permission prompt; no-op operations such as `true '/tmp was the locus'` trigger the permission prompt.
* **Interrupts legitimate agent actions before execution**: the agent can choose a command whose runtime behavior would not open the named path, but the pre-execution scanner still intercepts the action with a permission prompt based on the argument text alone.
* **May pollute the allowed-directory list if the default option is accepted**: the prompt's default option ("Yes, and add these directories to the allowed list") is labeled as adding the candidate string to the allowed list; based on that label, I would expect accepting it to persist non-path strings such as `/tmp is a sentence` as registered allowed directories. A user who casually accepts the default could then accumulate arbitrary English-prose fragments in their allowed-list configuration.
* **Can interrupt OS-development conversations** involving examples or prose that begin with `/`, similar to the impact described in #774 for the `session` tool.
* **Requires indirect workarounds**: routing all data through `echo` or the tested `awk` program-argument form, splitting strings to avoid a leading `/`, paraphrasing prose, or piping through unrelated transformations to obscure the leading slash.

## Environment

* GitHub Copilot CLI version: 1.0.48
* OS: Linux
* Use case: passing literal strings (English prose, JSON data, command examples) that incidentally begin with system-path-like substrings.

## Suggested Fix

One narrow fix would be to make the scanner command-semantics-aware:

1. Maintain a per-command path-argument-position table for common commands.
2. Apply the same observed behavior of passing `echo` arguments and the tested `awk` program-argument form to other known data-only / no-op commands such as `true`, `:`, and `printf`.
3. For commands that do have path-bearing argument positions, such as `cat`, `cp`, `mv`, or `chmod`, inspect only the positions that the command can actually use as filesystem paths.

A runtime filesystem-access signal, where available, could complement these lexical checks. A narrower available fix is to avoid applying path-access rules to known data-only argument positions.

Note: the scanner already passes arguments to `echo` and the tested `awk` form, and it passes the tested forms `true /foo`, `true /tmp`, and `true /xyz`. The fix is to extend comparable behavior to other data-only commands (`true`, `:`, `printf`) and to no-op builtins generally.

## Workaround

* Route data through `echo` — or through the tested `awk` program-argument form — instead of other commands when the data starts with `/`.
* Avoid any quoted argument whose first character is `/`, where possible. (Often impossible when the data is determined by the user's request.)
* Use heredoc redirection to a data-only command rather than quoted arguments. Note that heredoc-based workarounds may be affected by separate heredoc-body scanning behavior (https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/3334), so this workaround is not always reliable.

## Related

* https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/774 — Related report: a similar lexical-scanning failure mode rejects command-like words in text arguments passed to **non-bash tools** (e.g., the `session` tool). Both reports describe interception behavior when text containing pattern-matching tokens flows through contexts where the surrounding grammar makes clear the text is data, not the protected form the scanner pattern-matches against.
* https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/3334 — Related report: heredoc-body scanning misinterprets ordinary words like `kill`, `pkill`, `killall` in heredoc payload as shell `kill` commands without arguments. Similar lexical-scanning failure mode: text that looks like a protected pattern is rejected even though the surrounding grammar makes clear it is data.

---

**Note:** Together with #774 and #3334, this report describes interception behavior across multiple contexts that follow a similar lexical-scanning failure mode. The scanner already passes `echo` arguments, the tested `awk` form, and the tested unquoted paths `/foo`, `/tmp`, and `/xyz` for `true`, so a change to extend command-semantics awareness to other commands could be scoped specifically to a per-command path-argument-position table.

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.48.

issues.title: Rust rewrite regression on macOS: all native HTTPS requests fail with "bad certificate format" when com.apple.SecurityServer is not reachable (sandboxes)

labels.name: area:networking
labels.description: Proxy, SSL/TLS, certificates, corporate environments, and connectivity issues

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Starting with 1.0.93, Copilot CLI on macOS can't connect to its API when it runs inside a sandbox that denies the Mach service `com.apple.SecurityServer`. Sandboxes such as [nono](https://github.com/nolabs-ai/nono) deny this service so the agent can't read keychain secrets. Every native request (user lookup, `/models`, chat) fails with:

```text
[ERROR] Error loading models: Error: error sending request for url (https://copilot-api.<host>/models): client error (Connect): bad certificate format
```

The CLI then reports that the user isn't logged in. stderr also shows
`CSSM_ModuleLoad(): One or more parameters passed to a function were not valid.`

1.0.92 works in the same sandbox.

### Affected version

1.0.93 and 1.0.94 and 1.0.95-2 (1.0.92 works)

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

No third-party sandbox is needed. Denying only this one service with `sandbox-exec` is enough:

```bash
prof='(version 1)(allow default)(deny mach-lookup (global-name "com.apple.SecurityServer"))'
COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)" sandbox-exec -p "$prof" copilot --prefer-version 1.0.92 -p "Reply with just: hi"   # works
COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN="$(gh auth token)" sandbox-exec -p "$prof" copilot --prefer-version 1.0.93 -p "Reply with just: hi"   # bad certificate format
```

### Expected behavior

TLS works without access to the keychain daemon, like in 1.0.92.

### Additional context

From 1.0.93 on, more requests run in the native runtime (`runtime.node`). It contains two TLS stacks:
`rustls-platform-verifier` and `native-tls` (Security.framework / Secure Transport). The failing requests use
`native-tls`. Secure Transport needs `com.apple.SecurityServer` (the legacy CSSM path) to evaluate certificates and returns `errSSLBadCert` (-9808, "bad certificate format") when the service is not reachable.

I checked this with a small reqwest client, run under `sandbox-exec` denying one keychain-related Mach service at a time:

| Denied service                 | reqwest + native-tls | reqwest + rustls-platform-verifier |
|--------------------------------|----------------------|------------------------------------|
| none                           | OK                   | OK                                 |
| `com.apple.SecurityServer`     | -9808                | OK                                 |
| `com.apple.securityd`          | OK                   | OK                                 |
| `com.apple.security.keychaind` | OK                   | OK                                 |
| `com.apple.secd`               | OK                   | OK                                 |
| `com.apple.security.agent`     | OK                   | OK                                 |

Custom roots (`SSL_CERT_FILE` / `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`) make no difference: native-tls fails with and without them, and `rustls-platform-verifier` works with and without them.

Using `rustls-platform-verifier`, which is already bundled, for all native requests would fix this. Apple has
deprecated Secure Transport.

The same regression shows up elsewhere:

- #5081: 1.0.93 native model requests fail through a proxy on Windows (`UnknownIssuer`); reported fixed in 1.0.94-3. That fix does not cover this case: 1.0.94-4 still fails as described above.
- #4364: native Rust TLS on macOS rejects a private CA cert (-67901) after requests moved out of Node.

macOS 26.7.1 (Apple Silicon).

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Summary: In the main prompt composer, Ctrl-D behaves correctly (deletes the character under the cursor when the line is non-empty; only signals EOF/shutdown on an empty line — the behavior fixed some months ago). However, when the agent presents an  ask_user  elicitation form and I'm typing an answer into a form text field, pressing Ctrl-D immediately triggers "shutdown" and discards everything I'd typed into the form. It appears the non-empty-line guard applied to the main composer's Ctrl-D handler was never applied to the elicitation/form input widget.

Impact: Repeated loss of carefully composed answers (happened ~6 times in one session).

Severity: High — silent data loss of user input; unexpected shutdown.

Suggested fix: Route the form field's Ctrl-D through the same handler/guard as the main composer (non-empty line ⇒ delete-char; empty ⇒ ignore or blur, not global shutdown).

### Affected version

Copilot CLI 1.0.83, macOS (darwin-arm64)

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

Steps to reproduce:

1. Have the agent call a tool that shows an  ask_user  form with a free-text field.
2. Start typing a multi-line/long answer into the field.
3. Press Ctrl-D (e.g. out of habit, to delete a character).
4. Observe: the session shuts down / the form is torn down and the typed answer is lost.

### Expected behavior

Expected: In a form field, Ctrl-D should either delete the character under the cursor (matching the main composer) or be a no-op — it should NOT invoke global shutdown while a non-empty field has focus.

Actual: Ctrl-D invokes global shutdown regardless of field contents, discarding in-progress input.

### Describe the bug

An enabled marketplace-installed plugin extension is missing from `client.rpc.extensions.discover()` both before and after session creation, even though the extension runs in the session, appears in current tool metadata, and its tool executes successfully. In the same isolated environment, discovery does return a user-global extension.

The [Copilot SDK `extensions.discover()` API contract](https://github.com/github/copilot-sdk/blob/main/nodejs/src/generated/rpc.ts#L23660) describes discovery of user and enabled installed-plugin extensions from persisted Copilot home state. It also explicitly excludes launch-scoped additional plugins.

### Affected version

- GitHub Copilot CLI: `1.0.88` (Windows x64)
- Node.js: `v24.18.0` in the SDK harness
- SDK: `1.0.14-preview.1`, identified from SDK source-path labels in the CLI bundle. I did not independently verify package-resolution metadata.
- Reproduction uses a fresh, isolated `COPILOT_HOME`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a fresh `COPILOT_HOME` and a local marketplace containing a minimal plugin with one extension and one deterministic tool.
2. Install the marketplace plugin and confirm it is enabled:
   ```text
   copilot plugin marketplace add <local-marketplace-path>
   copilot plugin install minimal-discovery@<marketplace-name>
   copilot plugin list --json
   ```
3. Configure the SDK client to use the same Copilot home and CLI. Call `client.rpc.extensions.discover()`.
4. Create a session with extension loading enabled. Call `client.rpc.extensions.discover()` again, then inspect `session.rpc.extensions.list()` and `session.rpc.tools.getCurrentMetadata()`.
5. Execute the plugin’s deterministic tool from the session.
6. As a control, add a user-global extension to the same isolated home and repeat discovery.

### Expected behavior

The enabled marketplace-installed plugin extension should appear in global `extensions.discover()`, because it is an enabled installed-plugin extension persisted in the same Copilot home used by the SDK client. Launch-scoped additions are excluded by the documented contract; this marketplace fixture is installed in the isolated home, not supplied as a launch-scoped plugin directory.

### Additional context

Observed results:

| Fixture | `extensions.discover()` | Session/tool result |
|---|---|---|
| User-global extension | Present | Running; tool succeeds |
| Launch-scoped startup plugin | Empty | Running; tool succeeds |
| Minimal marketplace plugin | Empty before and after session creation | Enabled; extension running; tool metadata present; tool succeeds |

The launch-scoped result is consistent with the SDK contract. The discrepancy is that the enabled marketplace plugin is also absent from discovery despite being active and usable in-session.

The reproduction observed `load_and_augment` with an empty discovery list; this does not establish the cause of the discrepancy. The evidence identifies the behavior but not its internal cause.

Related history: `github/copilot-cli#3023` concerned plugin extensions not loading properly. In this reproduction, the plugin extension loads and executes; global discovery omits it.
