prs.title: feat(templates): open Control UI chat and create the agent without a plan
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Control UI Template Add waits for a plan, then can leave an empty agent when a declared plugin is disabled.

## User Impact

Add opens pending chat immediately and creates the agent with its original manifest, files, skills, bundled plugins and MCP servers without a plan/review step. Failed dependencies are reported instead of rolling back; source or workspace failure removes the new agent and chat. CLI plan/consent behavior is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Selects the chat path explicitly, reuses ordinary agent admission, preserves effective setup tools within explicit denies and operator ceilings, and leaves referenced plugins and automations for the following setup layer. The original workspace-root CLAW.md is reserved; a conflicting workspace declaration fails before Template writes. Its error now explains that nothing was kept and the publisher must move the conflicting file and publish a corrected release.

Warned skills or bundled plugins remain uninstalled and are reported. This does not bypass dependency trust checks.

## Evidence

### Current allocation-only repair

Published head `9ed5a58794db142be41f5e142e68a5cd92d72bd0` differs from `b7235cc095dff0eebd90cd268b2695ca96f98a08` only in this layer’s existing test-line allocation record: **211→338** for the actual **738 net test lines** above foundation. The unchanged global allowance is **400**. The actual ratchet fails with the old 211 allocation and passes with 338; no tests, assertions, product source, scanners or global budgets changed. The paired tests and performance inputs below are unchanged, so those results remain applicable rather than being represented as new executions. Exact-head hosted CI and completed review remain required.

### Retained source qualification

Head `b7235cc095dff0eebd90cd268b2695ca96f98a08` is restacked once above foundation `c1c471f63b56ad6e5908058d4bebf4e87e080454`. Generated validator conflicts were resolved by canonical regeneration, not hand-editing output. The CLI retains main's canonical scoped-package resolution and the leaf result contract. Git omitted the lazy-permission fixture repair because it is already upstream; unrelated source and all original worktrees are preserved.

- The complete strict paired performance command passes against exact foundation `c1c471f63b56ad6e5908058d4bebf4e87e080454`: `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-control-ui-performance-base.mts c1c471f63b56ad6e5908058d4bebf4e87e080454`. prs.title: feat(workboard): record optional claims, observations, and verification
prs.body:
Fixes #197450
Supersedes #161618

## What Problem This Solves

Workboard needs to distinguish worker claims, observed run outcomes, and checker verdicts without making evidence a requirement for completing work.

## User Impact

Workers can include optional claims when completing a card, and checkers can record what they checked and whether it was confirmed, disputed, or inconclusive. Completion and dependency scheduling keep their existing behavior, including for cards without evidence.

## Why This Change Was Made

Store the three record types separately with their source identities. Session lifecycle sync owns observations, and generic metadata writes cannot forge or remove evidence. Records are bounded to the newest four per kind within 6 KiB, and evidence only uses room the card's other records leave: near the 24 KiB card budget it drops its own oldest entries and never evicts proof, attempts, comments, or artifacts. `workboard_verify` returns an error when its record cannot fit; claims and observations that cannot fit are dropped without failing completion. No database migration is required; older versions may drop this optional evidence when writing a card.

## Evidence

- Regression test `store-evidence.test.ts`: fails on `63808cadb49` (a verification on a card near its budget evicted existing artifacts) and passes on this head. It also covers forged evidence through raw metadata and evidence surviving a later metadata write.
- Workboard suites: 192 tests passed across seven files (store, tools, lifecycle sync, plugin registration, Gateway, attempts, evidence). Extension and extension-test typechecks, type-aware lint, formatting, the line-cap ratchet, and the test-line ratchet passed locally.
- Test lines: the PR adds 27 net test lines. `config/test-lines-allocations/197471-workboard-result-evidence.txt` allocates the 9 lines past the ceiling; the regression test lives in its own file because `store.test.ts` is over its line cap.
- Isolated Gateway scenario with a stand-in model: completion with and without records, lifecycle observation from a real session run, checker verification, and rejection of forged observations through generic metadata. Not run against a live external model; the budget-fitting behavior is covered by the regression test, not this scenario.

prs.title: fix(templates): allow re-adding a deleted template agent
prs.body:
Closes #198475

## What Problem This Solves

Template Add fails with “deletion is in progress” when the same agent ID was previously deleted successfully.

## User Impact

Users can add the template again and receive a fresh agent and chat after deleting its previous agent.

## Why This Change Was Made

Chat preparation runs before config publication consumes the completed deletion record. Carry the existing creation claim through session admission and the history reader, so only the current creator can prepare that agent. Keep reader custody and cleanup with their existing owners, including checks that reject an ordinary request trying to reuse the creator's warm reader.

Reported and reproduced by @DonnieFi in the linked issue.

## Evidence

- Before the fix, the real add → production deletion → same-ID add regression fails with `Agent fixture-first deletion is in progress; new work is unavailable.`
- After the fix: **8 selected cases passed** across four files: recreation, fresh creation, post-commit revocation, pre-commit compensation, deletion-reader fences, reader cleanup/revocation, and session preemption. The recreation case also checks a fresh session, completed initialization, and rejection of a request outside the creation scope. Production SQLite workers were compiled by the canonical test wrapper.
- A separate pre-guard counterexample returned the recreated session to an outside-scope request. The same boundary now rejects it.
- Production core and Template test types passed; typed lint and formatting passed on all nine changed files, including the 700-line limits. Normal commit hooks passed without changing the reviewed bytes.
- Fresh independent desktop review over read-only SSH covered the complete nine-file patch against `ca026c1c`, with no unresolved P0–P2 findings. Final commit `3ccf4423095424a1e3cfc0f5a8510780bdd12baf` preserves that reviewed snapshot. CLI-based autoreview was not run.

<details>
<summary>Focused commands and limits</summary>

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.infra.config.ts src/templates/gateway-add-pending.test.ts src/infra/agent-database-readers.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --pool=forks -t 'admitted-recreated|admitted-applied|: revoked$|abort-before-commit$|runs every registered closer and keeps deleted databases closed until revived'
OPENCLAW_VITEST_NO_OUTPUT_TIMEOUT_MS=300000 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.runtime-config.config.ts src/config/sessions/session-transcript-worker-lanes.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --pool=forks -t 'revokes readers and joins cleanup.*pending=true, capable=true|retains reads dispatched after cleanup.*capable=true'
OPENCLAW_VITEST_NO_OUTPUT_TIMEOUT_MS=300000 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts src/sessions/session-controller.lifecycle.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --pool=forks -t '^preempt interrupts a captured subordinate effect before running the mutation$'
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo --noEmit
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.templates.json --noEmit
```

The first runtime-config attempt hit the wrapper's 120-second no-output deadline during cold compilation. The supported, finite 300-second budget completed both selected controls; that failed attempt remains recorded. Other cases in these files were intentionally unselected.

This is isolated production-service/SQLite proof. Live Gateway, browser and provider acceptance, and broad package/CI validation remain outside the local evidence.

</details>

prs.body:
Closes #198524

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: mocked Control UI E2E shards (`checks-ui-e2e`) hit the 20-minute test step limit when hourly `main` CI runs them on slower GitHub-hosted runners.

## User Impact

No product change. Hourly `main` and PR CI stop failing these shards on slow runners. Every test still runs. The step limit stays at 20 minutes.

## Why This Change Was Made

At six shards, the tallest cold shard is about 1,020 s: about 916 s of planned file time, plus about 30 s to build the Control UI bundle and launch Chromium, plus about 75 s to prepare the compiled-worker generation on the shard that holds the borrower files. Hosted AMD EPYC 7763 runners take 1.31-1.36 times as long as that, which passes 1,200 s. Details are in #198524.

- The compact plan runs nine Control UI shards (ten rows with the browser-extension row). The full-inventory plan already reserves thirteen rows, so the registration ceiling does not change.
- `guest-person-identities.e2e.test.ts` joins `UI_E2E_SHARED_WORKER_FILES`, so a run prepares the compiled-worker generation once instead of on two shards.

The sequencer and the weighted splitter are unchanged. The planner still leaves out the startup and preparation costs; at nine shards that gap is about 105 s on one shard, which the margin below absorbs.

Relation to open PRs: #197854 adds `route-asset-requests` and `control-ui-stale-build-reload` to the same borrower group. Combined with this PR, the list needs all entries; that is a one-line textual conflict. #198212 refreshes timings only.

## Evidence

- **Root cause, from CI logs.** I parsed the logs of 282 Control UI shard jobs in 47 hourly `main` runs (2026-11-11 to 2026-11-13). Timeouts: 35 of 63 jobs on hosted EPYC 7763 runners, 1 of 7 on hosted Xeon 8370C, 0 of 102 on Blacksmith, and 0 of 110 on other hosted CPUs. Replaying the sequencer on run 43501562872's recorded inventory reproduces its exact shard split, with 916 s of file weight per shard.
- **Tallest cold shard on the hourly-main inventory with the committed timings** (planned file time, plus 30 s startup on every shard, plus 75 s on the shard holding the borrower group):

  | Shards | Planned file time | Tallest cold shard | At 1.36x (EPYC 7763) |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 6 (`main`) | 916 s | 1,021 s | 1,389 s |
  | 9 (this PR) | 611 s | 716 s | 973 s |

  This is a projection, not a CI run of the new plan; this PR's CI is the first one.
- **Tests:**
  - `vitest-e2e-sharding` (8), `ci-ui-e2e-selection` (18) and `ci-ui-browser-dependencies` (6): all passed.
  - `ci-workflow-planning`: the cases covering the shard count (Control UI row counts, worker totals, the browser-owner routing matrix, Control UI gating) passed. 108 other cases in that file did not run locally: they need Bash 5+ and the local shell is Bash 3.2.
  - oxfmt and oxlint are clean on the changed files.
- **Other paths checked:**
  - The repository E2E sequencer, which shares the weighted splitter: its tests pass.

prs.title: fix(doctor): recognize git checkouts whose root ends in whitespace
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw doctor` classifies the install root with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` before offering the git update path. The result was `.trim()`ed, so a checkout whose directory legitimately ends in whitespace (for example `/srv/openclaw `) had its meaningful trailing space stripped, failed the root comparison, and was reported as "not a git checkout". The operator then got the package-manager guidance note and no git-update offer, even though the install is a source checkout. The same root-cause shape was approved for `openclaw update status` in #196654 and already shipped in `src/projects/project-checkout.ts`.

Precedent: #196654 (same one-line predicate fix at the update-check call site; this PR covers the doctor sibling)

## Why This Change Was Made

`detectOpenClawGitCheckout` in `src/commands/doctor-update.ts` now removes only Git's final LF record terminator (`replace(/\n$/, "")`), preserving filesystem characters in the checkout path, exactly matching the approved #196654 wording. Ordinary checkouts, aliases, separate Git directories, and non-checkouts keep the current classification and messages.

Production LOC is `+2/-1` in one file.

Classification: `behavior-completing`

## User Impact

A source checkout under a whitespace-suffixed directory is now recognized by `openclaw doctor`, so the "Update OpenClaw from git before running doctor?" prompt (and the resulting git update flow) appears as it does for ordinary checkouts. Ordinary paths are byte-for-byte unaffected; a path that merely looks similar after trimming no longer misclassifies.

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `4ec78cebcf3b`
- Current-main RED baseline: `76024435027d4ac4e51a58468bb1b5c4842d9fb0`
- Production entry: `maybeOfferUpdateBeforeDoctor` → `detectOpenClawGitCheckout` in `src/commands/doctor-update.ts`
- Canonical owner exercised: `detectOpenClawGitCheckout` at `src/commands/doctor-update.ts:32-34`
- Decision surface: the `"git" | "not-git" | "unknown"` classification that gates the git-update offer and the package-manager guidance note
- Recorder/readback boundary: `maybeOfferUpdateBeforeDoctor` return value plus the mocked `confirm`/`updateCommand` calls in the existing `src/commands/doctor-update.test.ts` harness
- Acceptance RED: on current main, a root of `/repo/source ` with `show-toplevel` returning `/repo/source \n` classifies as `not-git`: the offer resolves `false`, `confirm` is never called, and the package-manager note is printed
- Acceptance GREEN: on exact head, the same inputs classify as `git`: the offer resolves `true`, `confirm` is called once, and `updateCommand` receives `sourceUpdate: { root: "/repo/source " }`
- Legal control: the pre-existing table (another checkout, not-a-repository, missing git, inspection failure, host-owned install, non-interactive/non-TTY/declined gates, update-in-progress recursion) all passes unchanged — 11/11 prior cases green
- Cleanup: isolated vitest temp dirs only; no production Gateway, session, token, or config was touched

### Inspectable RED -> GREEN terminal trace

Vitest shard on the real runner (Node 24.22.1, docker `lexiflow-all`):

```text
# BASE (76024435027d) + new test, via node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/commands/doctor-update.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
FAIL src/commands/doctor-update.test.ts > offers the git update for a checkout whose root ends in whitespace
expected false to be true  (offer resolves false; confirm never called)
Tests  1 failed | 11 passed (12)
```

```text
# HEAD (4ec78cebcf3b), same command
Tests  12 passed (12)   Duration ~100s (compiled-worker preparation dominates)
```

```text
# Legal control on HEAD: pre-existing classification/guidance table + interaction gates
Tests  12 passed (12)
```

### Verification

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/commands/doctor-update.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 12/12 passed on exact head; RED reproduced on current main with only the new test
- Superseded: an earlier interactive-run gap was closed by the shipped-CLI proof below (produced on an unrestricted host with a real TTY); the vitest red/green at the classification boundary still stands.

### Scope and risk

- Production LOC: `+2/-1` (src/commands/doctor-update.ts)
- Test LOC: `+12` (src/commands/doctor-update.test.ts)
- Existing-solutions preflight: reuses the existing `resolveComparablePath` comparison and the approved `replace(/\n$/, "")` predicate from #196654; no new helper or export
- Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none (read-only discovery)

## Real behavior proof (shipped interactive CLI)

The review asked for terminal evidence from a physical whitespace-suffixed checkout. Reproduced with the compiled CLI (`node openclaw.mjs`, dist built from the pinned trees) running from a real Git checkout whose path ends in a meaningful space (`/tmp/oc-proof-doctor/leg2-head/openclaw-src `), inside a real TTY (tmux), with isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` and a real Git identity. The checkout's branch tracks an offline bare remote one empty commit ahead, so the offered update could actually fast-forward.

Base — current main `76024435027d4ac4e51a58468bb1b5c4842d9fb0`:

```text
◇ Update ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  This install is not a git checkout.                                   │
│  Run `openclaw update` to update via your package manager (npm/pnpm),  │
│  then rerun doctor.                                                    │
```

Doctor withholds the Git update offer and routes the operator to package-manager guidance.

Head — this PR `4ec78cebcf3b7a5b35ae8ec4ac00d18428fdbb0f`, same checkout shape and harness. The interactive prompt now appears (tmux capture):

```text
Doctor: maintenance admission
│
◆  Update OpenClaw from git before running doctor?
│  ● Yes / ○ No
```

Answering `Yes` enters the shipped source-update flow (same capture, after the answer):

```text
◇  Update OpenClaw from git before running doctor?
│  Yes
Doctor source update requires the accepted Git checkout.
```

prs.title: feat(cron): size automation run slots from the agent limit
prs.body:
Related: #196859

## What Problem This Solves

Due automations wait behind a fixed eight-run cap even when the host has unused agent capacity, and no setting lets an operator go past it.

## User Impact

- **The default is unchanged:** a new or upgraded install runs at most eight automations at once, with an eight-wide automation lane.
- `cron.dynamicConcurrency` (default `false`) turns on a shared limit. With it `true`, automation may start as many runs as `agents.defaults.maxConcurrent` minus the conversation turns in progress, and never fewer than eight. The default agent limit is `max(8, available CPU parallelism * 4)`, so this is 32 or more on most machines.
- The setting is a single on/off switch; it adds no number to tune, and it is not one of the settings Doctor retires.
- With the setting on, conversations start without waiting for automation. Running automations are not interrupted, so combined activity can briefly exceed the agent limit.
- With the setting on, waiting jobs are reconsidered when a run ends and within a minute of a conversation turn ending. With it off, the scheduler does no extra wakes.
- Condition checks stay three wide and hook dispatch stays eight wide in both modes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Sizing automation from the agent limit for everyone would raise eight to 32 or more on upgrade, so the shared limit is opt-in. With it on, the existing run queue decides how many automations may start from the conversation lane's configured width and active count, and the automation lane is as wide as that admission can reach. Keeping the budget at queue admission lets conversations start immediately.

A conversation turn ending frees capacity without any automation event, so with the setting on the scheduler looks at queued runs and fired conditions that wait for a slot within a minute.

Accepted tradeoffs (with the setting on):

- Only conversation-lane turns reduce automation's share; subagents, restart-recovery turns, and hooks do not.
- The eight-run floor can exceed a configured agent limit below eight.
- Lowering the agent limit during active automation can delay hooks until the shared budget drains.
- The automation lane also carries internal session events, plugin-hook turns, and channel join intros.
- Waiting demand causes a recheck each minute, including when another admission condition prevents a run.

Rechecking a requester's owner status when a delayed run starts is a separate fix and is not part of this PR.

## Evidence

Scheduler and lane regressions cover both modes:

- With an agent limit of 32 and 12 due jobs, eight start with the setting off and all twelve with it on.
- With an agent limit of 12, the automation lane is eight wide with the setting off and twelve with it on; hook dispatch is eight in both.
- With the setting on, an agent limit of 12 and two conversation turns in progress, ten automations run; a run ending passes its slot on, and a conversation turn ending gives its slot to the last queued automation on the next scheduler look.
- With the setting on, four conversation turns and eight long payloads, a fired condition that waits for a slot starts when only a conversation turn ends.
- The scheduler worker looks again within a minute while a run waits for a slot with the setting on, and not at all before the next due job with it off.

Four targeted files (49 tests) and the cron typecheck pass.

## Validation Limits

No live Gateway run covers this head. Real providers, config reloads, hook reservations, stored-data upgrade, and the full suite were not checked. The reported `ops-lifecycle.start-arm.test.ts` timeout is not addressed here.

prs.title: feat(doctor): check OpenClaw ID member roles and honor an optional roles default
prs.body:
Stacked on #197782. Review only the top four commits.

## What Problem This Solves

Doctor does not know that `gateway.roles.default` is optional or that OpenClaw ID member roles come from `gateway.roles.definitions`. With role definitions and no default, it wrongly reports that automations will lose owner access. It also has no check for a member whose role is not defined, for missing preset roles, or for role settings that have no effect.

## User Impact

User impact: `openclaw doctor` reports member-role problems in plain words and can write missing preset roles after asking.

- Fixed: with role definitions and no default, Doctor no longer reports that an automation "will lose access at the next run" or that owner status is unverified.
- New checks when OpenClaw ID is on:
  - a member whose role has no definition, with the member and role named;
  - a missing preset definition, with a repair that writes it. The repair asks first and says that the config file is rewritten as JSON and loses its comments;
  - a sandbox-required role held by a member, or set as the default, when no sandbox backend is available.
- New check for any Gateway: stored role assignments with no `gateway.roles.default`, which means named-role enforcement is off and the assignments have no effect.
- A Gateway with no `gateway.roles`, and one with a default set and OpenClaw ID off, get the same Doctor output as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The cron ownership checks and the replay script now ask whether named-role enforcement is on, as runtime admission does, and no longer test for the presence of `gateway.roles`.
- The member checks read the local claw record, so they work with the Gateway stopped. A claw that has never linked has no record and gets no warning. A record that exists and cannot be read, or whose member list is malformed, is reported with a fixed message that contains nothing from the record.
- The preset repair uses the same code as turning on OpenClaw ID: it adds only missing presets and never writes `default` or `assignments`.
- Docs for roles and OpenClaw ID describe the optional default, member presets, which role applies to a connection, and what a sandbox-required role does and does not contain.

## Evidence

- Doctor suites: 31 tests in 3 files pass at the review-fix commit. A reviewer separately ran 94 tests in 6 files, covering Doctor, activation presets, the config schema and Doctor's consent modes, all passing.
- Core and test typechecks, lint, format and ratchets pass.
- Independent review found no P0 or P1 and three P2 in the new member check: a corrupt record could put a fragment of an invite key into Doctor's output, a malformed member list passed silently, and a never-linked install got a false warning. The fourth commit fixes all three, with a test that plants a synthetic secret in a corrupt record and asserts none of it is printed. A second review found nothing.
- Two docs anchor checks fail the same way on `main`, in pages this PR does not touch.

Not run: a whole-Doctor output comparison against the parent, a repair while a live Gateway reloads, and real Docker or Podman probing.

prs.title: feat(openclaw-id): members with an admin role are administrators
prs.body:
Stacked on #197770. Review only the top three commits.

## What Problem This Solves

An owner can define an OpenClaw ID member role that includes `operator.admin`, and its members receive that scope. Several administrator actions still refuse such a member, because they check the kind of connection and not the scope. Gateway-managed GitHub publication also rechecks the requester's profile before each write, which does not see a member's role, so removing a member does not stop a publication they queued.

## User Impact

User impact: a member whose role includes `operator.admin` is treated as an administrator by the Gateway's administrator actions. Members without that scope gain nothing. No preset role includes it. OpenClaw ID is a Labs feature and is off by default.

Risk an owner should know: an administrator member can edit Gateway config, including role definitions and the OpenClaw ID switch.

What stays with owner devices: inviting, approving, removing, changing roles and admitting nodes all need an owner device signature. Linking, unlinking and recovery-kit steps stay owner-only. An administrator member keeps their own profile and is never treated as the shared owner profile.

Required action: a GitHub publication that a member queued before upgrading to this change is refused after the upgrade and must be requested again.

Turning on remote access as an administrator is not part of this PR. It is not implemented for any administrator sign-in yet.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Profile administration, model-account administration, personal files, mentions and the personal-profile scope check use the member's current role definition when the connection is a member with `operator.admin`. Before, they used the member profile's named role, which on a team Gateway is usually the restrictive default.
- A publication request records whether it came from a member connection. Before each GitHub write the Gateway rechecks current membership and the current role definition. A removed member, a downgraded role, a deleted definition or OpenClaw ID being turned off stops the write. If membership cannot be read, the request waits; it is never treated as authorized.
- A stored request from before this change has no recorded source. If its profile is an OpenClaw ID member profile, it is refused. Other stored requests behave as before.

## Evidence

- An audit of 169 administrator method descriptors plus HTTP surfaces found the connection-kind refusals fixed here. A reviewer spot-checked more than 15 actions across config, users, pairing, plugins, secrets, terminal, update and restart, cron, cloud dispatch and HTTP, and found no further exclusion and no path wrongly opened.
- Tests: an administrator member performs each fixed action and was refused before; operator and viewer members, nodes and a Tailscale user under a denying default are still refused; an administrator member cannot submit a membership change and is not the owner profile; publication stops after removal and downgrade; a pre-change stored request is refused for a member profile and still works for others.
- Final focused run: 12 files, 204 tests pass. Five typecheck lanes, lint, format, docs checks, import cycles and ratchets pass.
- Independent review of the first two commits found no P0 or P1 and one P2, the pre-change stored requests. The third commit fixes it. A second review of that commit found nothing.

Test lines: 596 added, 196 over the 400-line allowance, recorded in `config/test-lines-allocations/member-administrator-authority.txt`.

Not run: the full repository suite, real GitHub writes, browser tests, and an upgrade with a real queued publication.

prs.title: feat(openclaw-id): choose and change member roles on the Access page
prs.body:
Stacked on #197748. Review only the top three commits.

## What Problem This Solves

The Access page invite form offers two hardcoded roles, and a member's role cannot be changed after they join. With member roles defined in `gateway.roles.definitions`, an owner needs to pick from the roles their claw defines and to move a member to another role.

## User Impact

User impact: on the Access page an owner can invite someone into any role defined on the claw, change an existing member's role, and see and fix a member whose role is no longer defined. Operator stays the default. OpenClaw ID is a Labs feature and is off by default.

- Each role in the picker has a one-line summary: access to other people's sessions, whether a sandbox is required, and whether it has administrator access.
- A role that includes `operator.admin` is labelled, and inviting or moving someone into it asks for confirmation first.
- A role change is an owner-signed membership change. The member's connections close and they reconnect with the new role's limits, with no device approval prompt.
- A member whose role is not defined is shown as blocked, with the reason.

Known limit: a Viewer cannot open the Access page to see their own role, because loading plugin pages needs `operator.read`, which Viewer does not have. This PR does not widen Viewer.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The People data sent to owner devices carries a small summary per defined role, not whole definitions. Role names that are not valid protocol role names are listed as unavailable.
- The Gateway refuses a `set_role` to a role with no definition, including when the definition is deleted while the change is being saved.
- For an OpenClaw ID member, a re-issued device token follows the member's current role definition. Before, a browser first paired as a Viewer stayed capped at Viewer scopes and waited for device approval after an upgrade. Scopes are still intersected with the current definition on every connect, so an old token or pairing record cannot restore a role the member no longer has. Owner devices, nodes and other sign-ins are unchanged.
- The administrator confirmation is checked again against fresh role data at submit, so a role that gained administrator access after the page loaded cannot be used without confirmation.

## Evidence

- Gateway: 59 tests pass, including a browser that never held higher scopes being upgraded from Viewer to an administrator role and then downgraded, a non-owner being refused, and a role deleted during the save.
- Access page: 34 tests pass. One real-browser test of the page passes at this head.
- Typechecks for six projects, lint, style lint, i18n, format, docs links and the line ratchets pass.
- Two independent reviews. The first found two P1 and one P2: the upgrade case above, the stale confirmation, and the deleted-role race. All three are fixed in the second commit. The second review checked the pairing change and found no P0 or P1, and one stale test assertion, fixed in the third commit.

Screenshots (role list, administrator confirmation, change-role control on a blocked member, sandbox warning) were captured by the browser test with `OPENCLAW_CAPTURE_UI_PROOF=1`. They are not attached here yet.

Test lines: over the 400-line allowance, with the allocation recorded in `config/test-lines-allocations/access-role-picker.txt`.

Not run: the full repository suite and a live tunnel.

prs.title: feat(openclaw-id): guest member role with sandboxed session tools
prs.body:
Stacked on #197739. Review only the top two commits.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw ID members are either Operators, whose sessions run tools on the Gateway host, or Viewers, who cannot start work. An owner has no role for someone who should be able to work with the session's tools kept in a sandbox.

## User Impact

User impact: turning on OpenClaw ID also writes a `guest` role definition. A guest member reads shared sessions and starts their own work, and the exec and file tools of their sessions run in a per-person sandbox. Operator stays the default invite role. OpenClaw ID is a Labs feature and is off by default.

Important limit: a required sandbox contains a session's exec and file tools only. It does not contain Code Mode under the default `node` executor, CLI backends, or direct `node.invoke` calls by a role that also has `operator.write` or `operator.admin`. These limits apply to every sandbox-required role, named roles included, and are listed in `docs/gateway/operator-scopes.md`. With default settings a guest can reach the first two. Whether to close them for sandbox-required sessions, or to give the guest preset stricter defaults, is an open maintainer decision; this PR changes none of those paths.

A guest needs a Docker or Podman sandbox backend. Without one their runs fail; they never fall back to the host. The invite form warns when a sandbox-required role is selected and no backend is available.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The `guest` preset is `sessions.others: "view"`, `agents: "*"`, `scopes: ["operator.sessions.write"]`, `sandbox: "required"`. It is written with the other presets, only when missing.
- A member's sandbox requirement comes from the membership role, so it holds when named-role enforcement is off (definitions without `gateway.roles.default`), which is the normal state of a personal claw.
- Sessions a guest creates are stamped sandbox-required at creation. Forks, rewinds, spawned children, cron jobs and recovered runs keep the stamp. A guest cannot start a run in an existing host-execution session.
- The connection decides the role: a person who is a guest member and also has a non-sandboxed named role gets a sandboxed session over the member connection and an unsandboxed one over the other sign-in.
- The People data marks which roles require a sandbox and whether a backend is available. The backend probe runs only for that owner-only view.

## Evidence

- Focused runs: 127 Gateway tests, 36 cron tests, 24 UI tests and 23 People projection tests pass, with targeted typechecks, lint, format, docs checks and ratchets.
- New tests cover the preset being written; a guest's session stamped sandbox-required with enforcement on and off; forks, rewinds, children, cron and recovery keeping the requirement; refusal to run in a host-execution session; fail-closed with no backend; an operator member's sessions staying unsandboxed; and the two-sign-in case.
- These tests prove stamping, propagation and admission. They do not run a tool inside a real container.
- An independent review found the membership propagation consistent on every surface it listed, and reported the three uncontained paths above. The second commit corrects docs, UI copy and test names so nothing claims a guest has no host access.

Not run: a live Docker or Podman model run, a real restart and recovery cycle, the full repository suite.

prs.title: feat(llm-task): process bounded batches with per-item outcomes
prs.body:
Closes #177325

## What Problem This Solves

Workflows extracting or classifying several independent inputs need bounded fan-out and per-item outcomes without rebuilding that orchestration around every `llm-task` call.

## User Impact

Callers can submit 1–20 inputs, inspect ordered results, keep successful siblings, and explicitly resubmit selected unsuccessful inputs. Existing single-input behavior is unchanged. The optional plugin remains opt-in; this adds no core tool or persistent job service.

New feature proposal: maintainer acceptance of this optional-plugin API is requested, not assumed. `maxTokens` is per item, not a batch spending limit. Cancellation may occur after usage is incurred, and outer agent cancellation may suppress the response. This is not durable recovery or a provider's offline Batch API.

## Why This Change Was Made

`batch.items` shares the existing prompt, schema, routing, and host-authorized isolated-completion path. The existing public concurrency runner limits fan-out to 1–4 (default 2). A single deadline includes queue time, and invalid batch admission fails before inference. Each started input invokes the existing completion API once; the batch scheduler adds no retries and does not change underlying runtime/provider retry policy.

Failures return stable categories rather than raw provider exceptions or rejected model output. Results distinguish successful, failed, interrupted, and never-started items. No model credentials, file access, message delivery, new config settings, dependency changes, or storage migrations are added. Documentation explains manual retry and the non-persistent response boundary.

Related, not duplicated: #137450 adds native Codex output constraints; #161344 connects embedded Lobster stages. All-state PR searches for `llm-task` batch/parallel/concurrency found no matching batch implementation.

## Evidence

### Main integration — 2026-11-14 (`e7b0db2b1202d8ac867d7840e62ea03cb80eaedd`)

Merged main `db8cab9d3ea38f2f6583ab9350bc568f19d47839` into the original PR branch. GitHub now reports the PR can merge without conflicts. The sole content conflict was in the tool result path: default model selection stays with the completion runtime when no override is provided, and both single and batch calls return compact JSON text with the existing structured details intact.

- Main's existing compact-result assertion failed against the intermediate resolution because single-call text was still pretty printed. After restoring compact serialization, **all 38 tests across the three llm-task plugin test files passed** (Vitest 14.96s, wrapper wall time 19.04s). These tests cover default routing, schema forwarding, ordered results, partial failures, cancellation, and the shared deadline with fictional inputs.
- Extension production and test typechecks, typed lint for the three changed TypeScript files, formatting, plugin import boundaries, the test-line budget, and documentation link checks passed.
- Independent Codex autoreview completed for the five changed public files against `db8cab9d3ea38f2f6583ab9350bc568f19d47839`, with no accepted P0–P2 findings. It reviewed the supplied public runtime contracts and fictional tests; it did not run the tests or independently verify provider internals. Reviewed tree: `79a5648d43b221607ba281edd47096de78e4d5a6`.
- [GitHub CI for this commit](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43553709576) reports `action_required` with zero jobs started. Could a maintainer approve the pending fork workflow runs for this commit? The October CI and real-model Gateway evidence below belong to earlier commits. This follow-up did not exercise a live provider.

Maintainer acceptance of the optional batching API remains open. Only public source and fictional fixtures were used for the repair and review. Maintainer branch edits remain disabled.

### Previous main integration — 2026-10-27

Current integration head: `c83390ef3308588e834eb909d4abac13ec02a036`. This merge preserves original PR head `3b00bdbefd677053831294b62bbe4c978643bfda` and actual main `4d8806c8c2e297af9bc06f5cc73d4b0a3a8f949b` as its two parents.

Resolved four conflicts while retaining main's inlined model selection, simplified fixtures, native `outputSchema` forwarding, and documented same-route native-schema fallback. Every batch item keeps the shared isolated completion owner. The batch scheduler adds no retries; the runtime's existing fallback is not disabled or presented as a one-provider-request guarantee.

- All **36 tests across the three llm-task plugin files pass** on the integrated candidate (Vitest 60.40s; wrapper wall time 65.90s, including 35.21s initial worker compilation).
- The existing repeated-`$id` schema-forwarding test was run unchanged with the original PR production owner: **one failed / 25 skipped**, because `outputSchema` was undefined (76.66s wall time). Restoring the integrated owner byte-for-byte made the same test **one passed / 25 skipped** (30.19s). No new test, full-suite replay, or model call was added for this comparison.
- Targeted production and test typechecks passed (11.88s / 21.76s), along with typed lint, formatting, assertion/line-count ratchets and documentation links (16,044 checked; zero broken). An initial temporary typecheck configuration selected the wrong root; correcting that ignored verification configuration resolved its TS6059 setup error without a product/configuration change.
- Fresh canonical independent **P0–P2 review completed scoped-clean**, 1/1 pass with complete usage reporting. Static review and executed tests are separate evidence.
- Frozen contribution diff SHA-256 against that main: `705dc6845c8c5df2f1054b4170215b7ebf09605c50565e6344070c6565c17725`. Only the original five contribution files differ from main.

For the October 27 head, checks completed: 39 successful, 65 skipped, zero failed or pending checks were reported. [ClawSweeper's completed review of this exact integration head](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177326#issuecomment-6267939700) reports no actionable findings and accepts the original live proof together with the integration comparison; the remaining blocker is maintainer API acceptance. The separate hosted Codex attempt failed with an unknown service error, not a new code verdict. Earlier real-model/Gateway evidence below remains attributed to its original head and was **not rerun** for this integration. This work used only public source and fictional fixtures; no real account authorization, private material, raw logs, secrets or permission expansion. Maintainer acceptance of the optional batching API remains outstanding.

### Historical implementation and runtime proof

- Node 24, isolated source checkout, synthetic inputs only. The plugin lane passed **34 tests across 3 files**, including existing registration and Doctor contracts. Measured run: **30.71s wall time** including worker compilation.
- Production extension typecheck, extension test-type check, targeted typed lint, assertion-safety and line-cap ratchets, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed. After the final test-fixture type repair, the changed owner suite passed **24 tests in 12.85s wall time** (the other 10 plugin tests retain their unchanged-input passing evidence). Documentation audit: 15,720 internal links checked, zero broken.
- Regression scenarios: out-of-order completion with bounded concurrency; independent JSON/schema/provider failures without scheduler retry; no raw error leakage; admission rejected before any completion; completed/active/queued outcomes on cancellation and whole-batch timeout; strict-schema null placeholders preserve single-input behavior.
- Independent Codex autoreview completed for P0–P2 with **no actionable findings**. The review included the unchanged public concurrency owner; it did not execute project code or prove provider cancellation behavior.
- Previous-head (`fbd1b630`) [CI run 39254802659](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39254802659) passed, including production/test types, lint, changed boundary/extension tests, source contracts, guards, docs, and `openclaw/ci-gate`. The applicable dependency/security gates also passed. This is not presented as CI for the follow-up commit below; new-head CI is pending. Skipped unrelated lanes are not counted as executed.
- Additional generic prompt-prefix stability check did **not** complete: the unchanged agents-core test lane stalled after worker preparation and was terminated by its no-output watchdog (exit 143). It is not counted as passing. No timeout or assertion was weakened. PR CI remains the broader verification gate.

Implementation is intentionally limited to the existing optional plugin and two documentation files. The shared model prompt and completion-selection rules remain unchanged; the optional tool schema gains the batch argument. Maintainer edits are disabled at the author's request to avoid granting fork Actions/Secrets access; requested changes can be applied by the author.

### Deadline settlement follow-up (2026-10-21)

Follow-up head: `3b00bdbefd677053831294b62bbe4c978643bfda`. The initial live runs retained successful results and stopped queued work, but one timed run returned `completion_failed` for the slow item instead of `cancelled`. Its underlying provider/runtime failure cause was not established and is not inferred from the unit fixtures.

Investigation independently reproduced a missing batch-owner check: if completion resolves or rejects after `expiresAt` but before the timer callback executes, the old code can publish `ok` or `completion_failed` for that expired item. The fix checks the existing deadline at admission and both settlement paths, without changing the deadline, routing, credentials, provider runtime, or error-redaction policy. It keeps earlier successes and prevents queued dispatch.

- The two synthetic regressions both failed on `fbd1b630` for the intended late-result statuses (24 existing tests passed), then all **26 owner tests passed** after the repair: **15.72s wall time**, including cached worker preparation; test execution itself stayed below 5s. Existing registration/Doctor proof remains unchanged.
- Production and extension-test typechecks, targeted typed lint, formatting, assertion-safety and line-cap ratchets, and `git diff --check` passed. Checks were serialized after a build-lock conflict; the rejected concurrent attempts were infrastructure failures, not counted as passing.
- Fresh canonical Codex autoreview completed **P0–P2 scoped-clean** for this two-file follow-up, with no actionable findings. It did not independently run the tests or establish the cause of the earlier live runtime error.
- The follow-up removes duplicate admission-only deadline logic in favor of one shared check; only the existing tool and its test file changed (production +10/-8 lines, tests +35).

### Live behavior proof (2026-10-21)

Head: `3b00bdbefd677053831294b62bbe4c978643bfda`. Built with the repository's `qaRuntime` build profile and launched through `pnpm openclaw gateway run`. A fresh local-only Gateway used separate config, state, and workspace, with only the optional `llm-task` tool exposed. Requests used the production authenticated `POST /tools/invoke` entry point and the existing host-authorized isolated runtime with a real model, not mocked completions. Native session discovery and additional tool capabilities were disabled. No personal notes, conversations, private source, configuration, credentials, or raw authentication logs are included in this evidence.

Ordered partial outcomes: concurrency 2, shared schema requiring `category` to be `billing` or `technical`, and three synthetic inputs. The task classified an invoice and a startup problem; an explicit negative-control input requested `{"category":7}` to exercise schema rejection. The two successful results survived their sibling's failure and all IDs remained in submission order.

```json
{"http":200,"status":"completed","results":[{"id":"request-a","status":"ok","category":"billing"},{"id":"request-b","status":"error","error":"schema_mismatch"},{"id":"request-c","status":"ok","category":"technical"}]}
{"scenario":"ordered_partial_results","passed":true}
```

Whole-batch deadline: six inputs, concurrency 1, a 10,000ms whole-batch budget. The task requested a tiny JSON object for the fast/queued inputs and a deliberately long numeric-array response for the slow input. The unchanged diagnostic assertion requires retained completed results, an interrupted active item, and at least one never-started queued item in the same run. Only categories/statuses are exported, not the generated array. The clean final-head run passed both scenarios without temporary diagnostic instrumentation:

```json
{"gatewayReady":true,"head":"3b00bdbefd677053831294b62bbe4c978643bfda","cleanSource":true,"syntheticOnly":true}
{"http":200,"status":"timed_out","results":[{"id":"fast","status":"ok","category":"billing"},{"id":"slow","status":"cancelled"},{"id":"queued-1","status":"not_started"},{"id":"queued-2","status":"not_started"},{"id":"queued-3","status":"not_started"},{"id":"queued-4","status":"not_started"}]}
{"scenario":"whole_batch_deadline","elapsedMs":10019,"passed":true}
{"cleanup":"gateway_exited"}
```

The runtime proof is deliberately limited to this tool entry point and these synthetic scenarios, not model quality, a surrounding Lobster workflow, or a provider-side billing cutoff. A response reporting cancellation does not prove that the provider incurred no usage. Failures before the deadline/caller cancellation retain the existing `completion_failed` category; expired settlements are cancelled even when the deadline timer callback has not yet run.

The separate human owner decision is still outstanding: should `batch.items`/`batch.concurrency` and these per-item outcomes be accepted in the bundled optional plugin? No bot recommendation or passing check is presented as maintainer approval.

prs.title: fix(ui): replies wait up to 5 s to appear after switching back from another app
prs.body:
Closes #198451

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a reply that finished while the Control UI's connection was down takes up to 5 seconds to appear when you switch back to the browser from another app.

## User Impact

Switching back to the Control UI from another app reconnects right away, and a reply that finished while you were away shows up in well under a second instead of after 4–5 seconds.

## Why This Change Was Made

A browser window behind another app still counts as visible, so switching back fires only a window `focus` event, and the Control UI did not listen for it. Recovery waited for the next reachability probe, which runs every 4–5 seconds once the connection has failed for a while.

Window `focus` now goes through the same guarded recovery scheduler as `visibilitychange`, with the same checks (`recoveryAllowed`, `needsWakeReconnect`, no overlapping probes). A healthy connection is left alone, and retry backoff is unchanged. Focus does not run the service-worker update check, so switching apps adds no network request while connected.

This removes the wait after switching back; it does not change why or how often the connection drops.

## Evidence

- **Live Safari comparison:** [inspectable proof with screenshots and measured timings](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/198453#issuecomment-6871320515). On the current PR head in a private macOS/Safari 26.6.2 VM, the saved reply appeared 318 ms after window focus, versus 3,588 ms with the baseline activation module. Both runs stayed visible with zero visibility changes. The Gateway and UI were real; the model and proxy-injected interruption were local stand-ins. One accepted comparison pair.
- **Regression coverage:** `ui/src/app/gateway-page-activation.test.ts` exercises focus after sustained failed probes, immediate recovery, and skipping the service-worker refresh.
- **CI:** Applicable checks and the CI gate passed for `7fc90cc27ad0921cce7165f06f30a4673eda1955`, including UI tests, UI e2e, typecheck and lint.

**Not checked in the live comparison:**
- Chrome, Firefox or other browsers.
- A natural network drop, sleep/wake or Wi-Fi change.
- Real provider performance or repeated timing samples.
- The full test suite locally; the PR's CI supplies the broader checks.

prs.title: fix(codex): redact credentials in dynamic tool error content
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Thrown and failed Codex dynamic-tool paths were putting raw `errorMessage` / failure `message` text into `contentItems` without running it through `sanitizeToolResult`. Successful and middleware-adjusted result paths already redacted credentials, so a thrown tool error that embedded a bearer token (or similar secret) could still surface the credential in the app-server tool-result content.

**Configuration-dependent gap:** `formatToolExecutionErrorMessage` → `redactSensitiveText` uses configured `logging.redactPatterns` **in place of** defaults. Model-visible `sanitizeToolResult` / `redactModelVisibleToolPayloadText` **combines** custom patterns with built-in tool payload patterns. So under a nonmatching custom `redactPatterns` config, diagnostic/error formatting alone still leaks an unregistered synthetic bearer, while catch-path `sanitizeToolResult` keeps built-in bearer protection.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the shared `sanitizeToolResult` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime` on the two remaining failure content builders:

- `createCodexDynamicToolBridge` catch path in `dynamic-tools.ts` (thrown execution errors)
- `createFailedDynamicToolResponse` in `dynamic-tool-response-state.ts` (failed response factory)

Non-goals: no change to success-path redaction, budget truncation, or middleware ordering.

## User Impact

**Before:** A dynamic tool that threw (or failed via the shared failed-response helper) could return `contentItems` containing unsanitized credentials from the error text — especially when `logging.redactPatterns` replaced diagnostic defaults with patterns that do not cover bearer tokens.

**After:** Thrown/failed dynamic-tool error content is redacted with the same `sanitizeToolResult` used on successful result content (built-ins always apply for model-visible output).

## Evidence

- Production catch path: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.ts` now sets `text: sanitizeToolResult(errorMessage)`.
- Shared failed factory: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-response-state.ts` sanitizes the failure `message` before building `contentItems`.
- Regression: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts` spies `readLoggingConfig` with nonmatching `redactPatterns` `[String.raw`\bunrelated-only-[A-Za-z0-9]+\b`]`, asserts `formatToolExecutionErrorMessage` still contains the synthetic bearer (before), and asserts model-visible `contentItems` do not (after `sanitizeToolResult`). Mock restored in `finally`.
- Diagnostic harness: `scripts/codex-dynamic-tool-error-redact-proof.mts` prints the actual protocol response JSON.





### Custom-pattern regression (exact head `67505f4ca5c4`)

```text
Product head: 67505f4ca5c482f9eac9474cd0a6f25bf4afc2bd
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.thrown-error-redaction.test.ts --reporter=verbose
PASS redacts credentials from thrown dynamic tool error content items under custom logging patterns
```

Configures logging.redactPatterns=["never-match-custom-redact-pattern-141271"] via isolated OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH so formatToolExecutionErrorMessage still contains the synthetic bearer (defaults bypassed), then asserts the bridge response does not.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Thrown dynamic-tool error content could include unsanitized credentials when diagnostic redact patterns replace defaults.
- **Canonical reachability path:** `createCodexDynamicToolBridge` → tool `execute` throws → `formatToolExecutionErrorMessage` → catch builds `contentItems` with `sanitizeToolResult(errorMessage)` → `toCodexDynamicToolProtocolResponse`.
- **Boundary crossed:** Extension dynamic-tool error content → shared `sanitizeToolResult` from plugin-sdk agent-harness-runtime (model-visible policy merges built-ins).
- **Shared helper / provider constraint check:** Reused existing `sanitizeToolResult`; no new helper.
- **Real environment tested:** Local diagnostic harness against production `createCodexDynamicToolBridge` + `toCodexDynamicToolProtocolResponse` under custom `logging.redactPatterns`. **Live Codex binary was NOT used** — this records the actual protocol response object returned toward Codex, not a full app-server binary round-trip.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```text
$ node --import tsx scripts/codex-dynamic-tool-error-redact-proof.mts
# writes /workspace/codex-runtime-proof.txt
```

- **Evidence after fix (diagnostic transcript):**

```text
# Codex dynamic-tool thrown-error redaction diagnostic
# Generated: 2026-09-07T14:53:48.289Z (UTC)
# Proof surface: createCodexDynamicToolBridge → handleToolCall catch path
#               → toCodexDynamicToolProtocolResponse (JSON contentItems)
# Live Codex binary: NOT used (unavailable / not required for this harness)
# Synthetic credential only — non-usable fixture.

logging.redactPatterns = ["\\bunrelated-only-[A-Za-z0-9]+\\b"]
(nonmatching custom patterns replace diagnostic defaults;
 model-visible sanitizeToolResult merges built-ins.)

## Before catch-path sanitizeToolResult
formatToolExecutionErrorMessage(...) under custom redactPatterns:
{
  "formatted": "Upstream failed: Authorization: Bearer bearer-model-visible-credential-1234567890"
}
contains synthetic credential: true

sanitizeToolResult(formatted) alone (model-visible built-ins):
{
  "sanitizedAlone": "Upstream failed: Authorization: Bearer bearer…7890"
}
contains synthetic credential: false

## After fix: protocol response returned toward Codex app-server
toCodexDynamicToolProtocolResponse(createCodexDynamicToolBridge.handleToolCall(...)):
{
  "contentItems": [
    {
      "type": "inputText",
      "text": "Upstream failed: Authorization: Bearer bearer…7890"
    }
  ],
  "success": false
}

success: false
contentItems text contains synthetic credential: false
contentItems text contains "Authorization: Bearer": true

## Summary
- Under custom nonmatching redactPatterns, diagnostic formatting LEAKS the synthetic bearer.
- After sanitizeToolResult on the catch path, protocol contentItems do NOT contain it.
- This records the actual protocol response object, not Vitest expect() output.
```

- **Vitest (distinguishing regression):**

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts -t 'redacts credentials from thrown' --reporter=verbose
 ✓ |extension-codex| extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tools.test.ts > createCodexDynamicToolBridge > redacts credentials from thrown dynamic tool error content items 38ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed | 172 skipped (173)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 25.56s
```

- **Observed result after fix:** Under custom nonmatching `redactPatterns`, diagnostic formatting still contains the synthetic bearer; protocol `contentItems` after the catch-path sanitizer do not (`Authorization: Bearer bearer…7890`).
- **What was not tested:** Live Codex app-server / `@openai/codex` binary round-trip. Proof surface is the real bridge + protocol response object.
- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix

- [x] AI-assisted (Cursor)
- [x] I understand what the code does
- [x] Change is focused and does not mix unrelated concerns

prs.title: fix(gateway): back off queued media ownership waits
prs.body:
Related #198422

## What Problem This Solves

A queued generated-media `agentTurn` delivery that is still owned by agent recovery, or still waiting for its requester to finish, called `deferSessionDelivery(entry.id, 1_000)` and threw `SessionDeliveryDeferredError`. The delay was a fixed constant with no backoff, no attempt or age cap, and no dead-letter path, so a permanently stuck entry re-deferred once per second forever. Each defer upserts the whole `delivery_queue_entries` row and every non-partial index, which is why one such row accounted for roughly 89% of that host's state WAL (`~5-6 GB/day` of writes).

## User Impact

A stuck delivery keeps its place in the queue — it is not dropped and it stays visible to the existing health/queue surfaces — but its ownership wait now backs off with queue age and settles at one attempt per minute. Because one defer is one full-row upsert, the scheduled delay is the row-rewrite interval:

| queue row age | defer delay / row rewrite interval (main) | defer delay / row rewrite interval (this branch) | rewrites/hour (main → branch) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fresh | 1 s | 1 s | 3,600 → 3,600 |
| 1 min | 1 s | 2 s | 3,600 → 1,800 |
| 2 min | 1 s | 4 s | 3,600 → 900 |
| 5 min | 1 s | 32 s | 3,600 → 113 |
| 6 min and older | 1 s | 60 s | 3,600 → **60** |

Steady-state writes from a permanently stuck entry therefore drop by 60×, while a delivery that becomes deliverable again is still picked up within at most a minute.

## Why This Change Was Made

The report's first suggested fix: back the ownership defer off instead of retrying on a fixed interval. `agentDeliveryOwnershipRetryDelayMs` derives the step from `entry.enqueuedAt`, which the record already carries, so no new queue state, column, or migration is needed and a restart resumes the same schedule. Both ownership defer sites use it: the transcript-write wait for the running turn, and the outbound-owner wait.

Deliberately not included: dead-lettering after an age cap. Dropping a delivery is a product decision about user-visible message loss, and the report's own other suggestions (update only `available_at` on a defer, log first-defer/dead-letter) are independent changes; this PR keeps the entry queued and only bounds the retry rate.

## Evidence

### 1. Live Gateway A/B — same four stuck deliveries, `upstream/main` vs this branch

Method: `openclaw gateway run --port 28790` on an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, built twice (`gatewayWatch` profile) — once at `c246818` and once with only `src/gateway/server-restart-sentinel-agent-delivery.ts` reverted to main. Four durable `agentTurn` generated-media deliveries were staged in `delivery_queue_entries` at queue ages 0/2/5/10 min. Each has an external route and a pending outbound receipt held by a live producer claim (`recovery_state=producer_claimed`, `requiresProducerClaim`, retention object) — the production "still owned by outbound delivery recovery" state — so every due attempt reaches the real `deferSessionDelivery` call site. The queue was then sampled read-only every 150 ms: each `updated_at` change is one full row rewrite, and `available_at − updated_at` is the delay the production code passed to the defer.

| staged age | first defer (main) | first defer (this branch) | defer delays observed (this branch) | row rewrites in 229 s (main → branch) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fresh (9 s) | 1 s | 1 s | 1 s ×32 → 2 s ×29 → 4 s ×10 → 8 s ×7 | 178 → 78 |
| 2 min (129 s) | 1 s | 4 s | 4 s ×9 → 8 s ×8 → 16 s ×3 → 32 s ×2 | 178 → 22 |
| 5 min (309 s) | 1 s | 32 s | 32 s ×2 → 60 s ×3 | 178 → 5 |
| 10 min (609 s) | 1 s | 60 s | 60 s ×4 | 179 → 4 |

The 10-minute-old delivery is the steady-state case from the report: 4 row rewrites in 229 s (≈60/hour) instead of 179 (≈2,800/hour measured, 3,600/hour by construction).

**Stays queued across restart.** The Gateway was stopped mid-run and started again 6 s later (shaded band in the image). The 10-minute-old delivery deferred at 60 s before the restart and at 60 s after it — same row, still `pending`, `retry_count` still `0` (a deferred ownership wait does not consume the retry budget).

**Settles when ownership clears.** Marking the four receipts `completed` ended the deferrals: each delivery settled (`status=completed`) on its next due attempt, at most one delay step (≤60 s) later, and no new rewrites followed.

![PR 198472 live Gateway proof: main rewrites every stuck delivery once per second; the branch ramps 1 s → 60 s, survives a restart, and settles once the outbound owner clears](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wr-web/openclaw/proof-assets/198472/ownership-backoff-proof.png)

### 2. Scheduled delay read back from the real queue drain

Independent measurement on the same head, driven through the production drain against a real isolated state database: `enqueueClaimedSessionDelivery` seeds a produced-media `agentTurn`, its queue row is aged (the row's `enqueued_at` is rewritten in the state DB), the real `drainPendingSessionDelivery` calls the production `deliverQueuedSessionDelivery`, and the scheduled `availableAt - now` is read back through `loadPendingSessionDelivery`.

| queue row age | main scheduled delay | this branch scheduled delay |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 71 s | 997 ms | 1 997 ms |
| 370 s | 997 ms | 59 998 ms |

```
# main
{"rowEnqueuedAt":1794627666059,"ageMs":69331,"scheduledDelayMs":997,"status":null}
{"rowEnqueuedAt":1794627325799,"ageMs":369078,"scheduledDelayMs":997,"status":null}

# this branch
{"rowEnqueuedAt":1794627577138,"ageMs":70936,"scheduledDelayMs":1997,"status":null}
{"rowEnqueuedAt":1794627232440,"ageMs":370534,"scheduledDelayMs":59998,"status":null}
```

### 3. Red/green at the production defer sites

`src/gateway/server-restart-sentinel-agent-delivery.test.ts` drives `deliverQueuedGeneratedMediaCompletion` itself — both defer sites (running-turn transcript wait and outbound-owner wait) — and asserts the exact delay handed to `deferSessionDelivery`. It does not import the helper, so it exercises the call sites rather than the calculation.

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/server-restart-sentinel-agent-delivery.test.ts
```

| source under test | fresh | 2 min | 10 min | 6 h |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `upstream/main` | 1,000 ms ✅ | 1,000 ms ❌ (expected 4,000) | 1,000 ms ❌ (expected 60,000) | 1,000 ms ❌ (expected 60,000) |
| this branch | 1,000 ms ✅ | 4,000 ms ✅ | 60,000 ms ✅ | 60,000 ms ✅ |

On main the aged cases fail on the assertion (`expected 60000, received 1000`), not on a missing export — reverting either call site to the constant makes the suite red again.

Gates run locally against `upstream/main`: oxfmt, oxlint, `run-tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json`, `check:line-cap-ratchet`, `check:test-lines-ratchet` (net +113, allowance 400), `check:madge-import-cycles` (0 cycles).

## What was not tested

- Nothing was run against the reporter's actual affected production state database. The staged deliveries reproduce the source path (same queue records, same scheduler, same defer call), but that `~5-6 GB/day` WAL host was not available; a maintainer with it can sample `delivery_queue_entries.updated_at` before and after.
- The running-turn transcript wait was exercised at the production call site with an in-process controller-work stub, not live with a real long-running turn; both sites share the same delay helper, and the outbound site was driven live end-to-end.
- The report's other two suggestions (defer updating only `available_at`, and info-level first-defer/dead-letter logging) are not implemented here.

prs.title: perf(sessions): encode delivery session bytes once
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Session-event delivery variants reuse their session JSON string but repeatedly encode it to UTF-8. Both the prepared envelope serializer and the fallback broadcaster do this, including for large session rows.

## User Impact

Session broadcasts perform less repeated UTF-8 work. Uncompressed frame bytes, recipient authority, delivery histories, ordering and scheduling remain unchanged. No configuration or migration changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The delivery already owns the exact history-specific session representation. Its lazy serializer now owns the UTF-8 session field instead of a string. Both envelope paths consume those bytes, and frame assembly preserves their segment identity instead of assuming one or three payload segments and copying them into recipient-specific buffers.

Production delta: **net -6 lines**. No cross-publication cache or new retention policy. The existing benchmark now uses the real broadcaster/frame assembly instead of maintaining a copied encoder.

## Evidence

The mixed-authority/history regression observes **10 session encodes on main versus 6 with this change**: two authorities, each with two delta histories and one legacy delivery. Capability variants share those six deliveries. The final six-encode assertion was rerun against the baseline and fails with ten encodes in all four producer cases. All six tests in that file pass on the candidate (18.75 s Vitest / 25.21 s wrapper). Three focused transport/serialization files also pass (**46 tests, 1 skipped**), covering ordinary/shared-message frames, compression round trips, byte accounting, and transport ownership. Script-types, root test-types, Gateway-root test-types and scoped lint/format pass.

The owner replay uses one changing session with 128 KiB of UTF-8 last-message text, 70 recipients, eight prepared audience identities, distinct viewer keys, 40/20/10 view-history cohorts and legacy/delta/field-reference capabilities. Presentation/admission and socket sinks are synthetic; projection, delivery planning, broadcaster and frame assembly are real. Exact complete uncompressed frame digests match. Deflate representation can differ with segment boundaries; existing codec tests prove decoded bytes and size accounting. This is not a whole-Gateway or production stall measurement.

| Owner metric | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| CPU/fan-out, paired mean | 18.038 ms | 17.314 ms (**-4.0%**) |
| Sampled V8 allocation/fan-out | 20.197 MiB | 19.091 MiB (**-5.5%**) |
| UTF-8 bytes encoded/fan-out | 5.489 MiB | 4.861 MiB (**-11.4%**) |
| Session encodes/fan-out | 31.164 | 26.458 |
| p50, pair 1 / pair 2 | 18.274 / 18.685 ms | 17.821 / 17.532 ms |
| p99, pair 1 / pair 2 | 71.989 / 184.159 ms | 25.239 / 52.203 ms |
| Max, pair 1 / pair 2 | 143.613 / 402.979 ms | 54.370 / 94.332 ms |
| Fan-outs over 180 ms, pair 1 / pair 2 | 0 / 10 | 0 / 0 |

Timing: **1,000 samples per arm per pair**, serial AB/BA (2,000 per side). Separate collected-allocation passes: **200 per arm per pair** (400 per side). CPU improved 3.0% and 5.0% in the respective pairs. A/A (1,000 each): CPU **17.721 / 17.746 ms**, p99 **26.105 / 25.413 ms**, no fan-outs over 180 ms. Wall tails varied substantially with host contention; these results do not establish elimination of production stalls. The baseline encoded 4,706 delivery groups twice across 1,000 fan-outs; the candidate encoded every delivery group once. Total string-encoding calls increase from 63.387 to 89.845 per fan-out because small prefixes are separate; encoded byte volume and measured CPU/allocation fall.

Timing host load (1-minute, start/end): baseline **13.64/17.84**, **35.23/29.91**; candidate **16.85/16.52**, **18.32/31.42**. Post-GC heap was **36.8 MiB on every arm**, context only. Raw per-arm RSS/heap and maxima are retained in the measurement output.

A negative control with distinct history tokens for every recipient showed no encoded-byte saving. The benefit is reuse across capability variants of a delivery, not deduplication of unrelated delivery histories. The replay includes JSON escaping and multibyte text; V8 sampled allocation excludes external Buffer backing storage, so encoded-byte counts are reported separately.

Command: `node --expose-gc --experimental-test-module-mocks --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/session-event-envelope-measure.ts --events 1000 --clients 70 --audiences 8 --distinct-viewers --source-revisions --session-kib 128 --reuse-envelope --encode-envelopes`. Baseline uses saved projection and broadcaster sources from `8ebbcaf62a27` via `--owner` and `--broadcast-owner`. Allocation uses `--events 200 --allocations`. CPU/allocation include synthetic row replacement per publication; instrumented digest/count replays are separate.

Plain Codex branch autoreview passed: **scoped-clean at default P0**, with no provider/model/environment overrides. [Exact-head CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43550918762) for `1f9ac03d2930408460f20abc31ca3c8e4948a853`: 45 jobs passed, 27 skipped; both required CI gates are green. Ready for maintainer review; not merged.

Doctor schema-guard tests construct a current agent database and then convert it to a historical fixture for every case. This candidate reuses the existing historical fixture owner directly.

The source removes 29 redundant current-schema constructions and conversions while retaining the existing tests. This is less construction work; it is not by itself proof of lower elapsed time or CI cost. prs.title: fix: defer release pruning until deployment verification completes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Release pruning ran before build/publication while the incumbent Gateway was still serving. During the r324 → r325 Team deployment at 2026-11-14 02:27–02:36Z, deleting an old sealed dist/node_modules tree coincided with a 47.8 s btrfs commit at 02:31:22Z, roughly 80–90 s of readyz probe timeouts, and a 121 s agent-database writer wait. An earlier commit in the same phase took 11.3 s. The subsequent build preflight required 66.9 GB and 712,759 inodes.

## User Impact

Deployments no longer prune releases in the pre-build window. Cleanup uses the existing path after cutover, full verification, verification marking, and activation-journal retirement; explicit `--cleanup` remains available. Retention is unchanged: current/previous, the newest three verified releases, pins, and journal references stay protected. Insufficient capacity refuses preparation so cleanup can be scheduled separately.

Post-cutover pruning can still cause a host-wide commit stall and delay other I/O, including the serving Gateway. This change removes overlap with deployment drain and verification; it does not eliminate the underlying filesystem stall.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remove the pre-build cleanup call and its now-unused selected-candidate protection argument. Reuse the existing post-acceptance owner rather than adding a reaper, config, cache, or new deletion policy. Production LOC is net −4. The change preserves lane 2457's #198303, #198501, #198513, and #198574.

A paced-deletion experiment was explicitly rejected after measurement. Five interleaved btrfs A/B pairs, preceded by two A/A controls, used fresh 360,000-file sealed release trees alongside a physically allocated ~35 GiB synthetic SQLite database with 5,000 sessions, 62,000 workspace files / 1.14 GB, and a concurrent FULL/WAL writer. No Team data was copied and Team was not accessed or modified.

| Metric | Original deletion | Rejected paced deletion |
|---|---:|---:|
| Median owner wall time | 4.39 s | 146.16 s |
| Median owner CPU | 4.29 s | 8.84 s |
| Median sampled allocation | 2.00 MiB | 142.97 MiB |
| Median peak pinned metadata | 225.64 MiB | 144.58 MiB |
| Median maximum btrfs commit | 43 ms | 40 ms |
| Worst measured btrfs commit | 83 ms | 154 ms |

Pacing doubled CPU, allocated approximately 143 MiB, and showed no convincing commit-latency gain. It is absent from this PR. A/A maximum commit times varied 206 → 48 ms; the fresh synthetic filesystem did not reproduce the production 47.8 s commit. The lead approved landing the ordering fix alone.

Other pre-cutover work was inspected: installation already uses `clone-or-copy`, staging uses `cp --reflink=auto`, and Git fetches the selected commit shallowly. Build-tree cleanup is unchanged. Prior lane 960 found dependency-tree reuse slower than fresh installation, and lane 1279 already removed filesystem-wide sync from sealing.

## Evidence

- The production-path deployment fixture fails against base `9bf3e79c823a51b098ab892d2f8f505931cd5671`: pruning observes `accepted:false`. With this fix, every quarantine/prune call observes full acceptance and no activation journal, and the obsolete tree is removed.
- Focused disposable Linux tests cover deployment ordering and retention, including failed releases, current/previous/verified/pinned/journal references, and cross-filesystem retention.
- Two existing test wrappers now preserve FD9 when delegating to the real library. Their missing deployment lock reproduces on the exact base and was introduced by `3efe1deca653` / #193647. Production lock enforcement is unchanged.
- All nine focused disposable Linux tests pass. `pnpm check:changed`, Bash syntax, and `git diff --check` pass. Independent Codex autoreview of the final local snapshot against base `9bf3e79c823a51b098ab892d2f8f505931cd5671` is scoped-clean at P0–P2 with no actionable findings. Exact-head CI and zero open ClawSweeper items are required before native `scripts/pr` landing.
