issues.body:
### Affected component security/sandbox ### Severity S1 - workflow blocked ### Current behavior `generate_policy` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/seatbelt.rs:272-380`) builds the SBPL profile inside a Rust raw string (`r#"..."#`), and the rule commented "Allow reading user home for tool configs" is written as ```text (allow file-read* (regex #"^/Users/[^/]+/\\.")) ``` (`seatbelt.rs:341-343`). A raw string keeps both backslashes, so sandbox-exec receives `\\.`. In an SBPL `#"..."` regex literal `\\` is an escaped backslash and `.` is any character, so the rule matches `/Users//\x...` and never a dotfile; Apple's own profiles write `\.`. The rule has been this way since the profile was added (`32edadc256`, #4592). Verified on macOS 26.5.1 with a profile that reproduces the generated rules (system subpaths, temp directories, `process-exec`): | Probe | generated rule (`\\.`) | corrected rule (`\.`) | no rule | |---|---|---|---| | `wc -c ~/.actrc` | `open: Operation not permitted` | `93` | `open: Operation not permitted` | | `wc -c ~/Applications` (control, no dot) | denied | denied | denied | | `~/.cargo/bin/cargo --version` | `execvp() ... Operation not permitted` | launches | denied | Seatbelt is the default backend on macOS: `SandboxBackend::Auto` is the default (`schema.rs:19920-19923`) and auto-detection selects sandbox-exec whenever `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` exists (`detect.rs:370-376`), so every stock macOS install runs the shell tool under this profile. Consequence: anything installed or configured under a dot directory is unreachable for sandboxed commands: rustup's `cargo` (`~/.cargo/bin`, and `~/.cargo/registry` for any build), nvm's `node` and `npm` (`~/.nvm`), pyenv (`~/.pyenv`), uv and pipx tools (`~/.local/bin`), and the configs `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.cargo/config.toml`. `cargo`, `node`, `npm`, `python` and `pip` are in the default allowlist (`policy.rs:443-447`). The sandboxing docs attribute the resulting "Operation not permitted" errors to tools that "don't cooperate with Seatbelt's file-access rules" and recommend switching to Docker (`docs/book/src/security/sandboxing.md:189`). **Security constraint on the fix.** The rule as intended grants read access to every dotfile and dot-directory of every account under `/Users`, including `~/.ssh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.aws` and `~/.config` (the default `forbidden_paths`) and `~/.zsh_history`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.docker/config.json`. The shell path scanner cannot see inside a workspace script, so `file_write read.py` followed by the allowlisted `python read.py` reads `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` with no policy refusal; only the sandbox can stop it, and the Linux Landlock backend grants no home access at all (`landlock.rs:105-160`: system paths and policy roots only). Today the broken regex accidentally gives macOS the stronger posture. A one-character fix would hand the sandbox exactly the exception the policy forbids. (A related consequence: the `~/.zshenv` hook in the companion issue is currently blocked under Seatbelt unless the home directory is inside a policy root.) ### Expected behavior The grant does what its comment says, scoped so it cannot contradict `forbidden_paths`: - Fix the escaping (`\.`), restrict the match to the daemon's own home directory rather than `/Users/[^/]+`, and either enumerate the tool directories that need it (`~/.cargo`, `~/.rustup`, `~/.nvm`, `~/.pyenv`, `~/.local`, `~/.npm`, `~/.gitconfig`, `~/.npmrc`) or keep the blanket dotfile grant and follow it with `(deny file-read* (subpath ...))` for every resolved `forbidden_paths` entry. Seatbelt applies the last matching rule, which the profile already relies on (`seatbelt.rs:290-292`). - An integration test gated on `SANDBOX_EXEC_PATH` like the existing ones (`seatbelt.rs:792-800`): a dotfile under `$HOME` outside `forbidden_paths` is readable, a fixture under `~/.ssh` is not, and `cargo --version` from `~/.cargo/bin` launches. - Replace the docs paragraph that blames the tools. ### Steps to reproduce ```bash # macOS with sandbox-exec and a rustup toolchain (cargo in ~/.cargo/bin) cat > /tmp/zc.sb <<'SB' (version 1) (deny default) (allow process-exec) (allow process-fork) (allow signal (target self)) (allow file-read* (subpath "/usr") (subpath "/bin") (subpath "/sbin") (subpath "/Library") (subpath "/System") (subpath "/private/var") (subpath "/dev") (subpath "/etc") (subpath "/Applications") (subpath "/opt") (literal "/") (subpath "/var")) (allow file-read* (subpath "/tmp")) (allow file-read* (subpath "/private/tmp")) (allow file-read* (regex #"^/private/var/folders/")) (allow file-read* (regex #"^/Users/[^/]+/\\.")) (allow file-write* (subpath "/dev/null")) (allow sysctl-read) (allow mach-task-name) SB sandbox-exec -f /tmp/zc.sb /usr/bin/wc -c ~/.zshrc # Operation not permitted sandbox-exec -f /tmp/zc.sb ~/.cargo/bin/cargo --version # execvp() failed: Operation not permitted sed -i '' 's|/\\\\\\\\\.|/\\\\.|' /tmp/zc.sb # change \\. to \. sandbox-exec -f /tmp/zc.sb /usr/bin/wc -c ~/.zshrc # byte count printed # Through ZeroClaw: default config on macOS, shell "cargo --version" -> Operation not permitted ``` ### Impact **Attack vector.** None for the defect itself: it fails closed. The security content is the constraint on the fix described above. **Likelihood.** Every macOS install whose developer tools come from rustup, nvm, pyenv, uv or pipx, which is most developer Macs, hits this on the first `cargo`, `node` or `python` command through the shell tool. The docs steer those users to Docker instead of naming the cause. **Data exposed.** None today. A naive fix exposes `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg`, shell history and credential dotfiles to any allowlisted interpreter running a workspace script, on the platform whose sandbox is meant to be the backstop. **Data flow** ```mermaid flowchart LR R["Rust raw string r#...#
(regex #"^/Users/[^/]+/\\.")"] --> P["generated .sb profile
contains \\. (two backslashes)"] P --> I["SBPL regex meaning:
escaped backslash, then any character"] I --> X["never matches /Users/name/.cargo, ~/.gitconfig, ~/.nvm ..."] X --> D["cargo, node, python from dot directories:
execvp Operation not permitted"] F["naive fix: \\. becomes \."] --> G["sandbox grants every dotfile under /Users/*
including ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg, ~/.config"] G --> H["file_write read.py + allowlisted python read.py
reads ~/.ssh/id_ed25519, policy never sees the path"] classDef bad fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b00000,color:#000 classDef warn fill:#fff4d6,stroke:#b36b00,color:#000 class P,I,X,D bad class G,H warn ``` **Attack path if fixed naively** ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber participant X as Untrusted content participant M as Model participant P as SecurityPolicy participant S as sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) participant F as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 X->>M: injected instruction M->>P: file_write read.py (prints the key file) P-->>M: allowed, in-workspace write M->>P: shell "python read.py" P-->>M: allowed, python is allowlisted and read.py is a workspace path S->>F: open() under the corrected blanket dotfile grant F-->>M: key material in the tool output Note over P: forbidden_paths never evaluated: the path lives inside the script ``` **Evidence:** code reading of master `1c1cd118ac` and the experiments above, executed on this Mac (macOS 26.5.1). ### Logs / stack traces _No response_ ### ZeroClaw version master `1c1cd118ac` (v0.8.7) ### Rust version 1.98.0 (CI toolchain) ### Operating system macOS 26.5.1 (any macOS with sandbox-exec) ### Regression? No, first-time setup ### Pre-flight checks - [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: Telegram channel ignores edited_message updates — mention added via edit is never seen
issues.body:
## Summary

The Telegram listener only ever reads `update["message"]`. Updates of type `edited_message` — which Telegram emits when a user edits a previously sent message — are never inspected: no gate re-evaluation, no passive-context recording, no trace event, and the long-poll offset still advances past them. As a result, any information added by an edit is invisible to the agent until some *new* message triggers processing.

## Concrete scenario (observed in production)

1. Group chat with a channel configured `mention_only = true` and `passive_group_context = true`.
2. User sends a long message **without** @-mentioning the bot → correctly recorded as passive context.
3. User **edits** that message to append `@bot_username <request>` — the exact signal the mention gate is built to catch.
4. Daemon never sees the edit: no `processing inbound message`, no mention gate run, no response. The group experiences a silent ~25-minute gap until an unrelated fresh message finally mentions the bot (which then also had to carry the whole accumulated passive context in one turn).

Trace evidence: the recorded inbound carries the original text (no mention); the user's edit (visible in the client) never produces any trace line — `edited_message` handling is absent from `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/telegram.rs` entirely.

## Why it matters

Editing a message to add the bot's mention is a natural user behavior — arguably *more* natural than re-sending, because it keeps the conversation tidy. With `mention_only`, this turns the bot deaf precisely in the case the gate exists for. It also silently drops any factual correction a user makes by editing (the agent keeps working from the stale text).

## Possible directions (maintainers' call)

- Minimal: treat an edited message whose new text now passes the mention gate as a fresh inbound message (with an `edited` marker so history handling can decide whether to replace or append).
- Fuller: maintain a message_id-indexed shadow of group messages so an edit can replace the previous passive entry instead of duplicating context.
- Out of scope: applying edits to already *processed* turns (history rewrite) — probably worth explicitly documenting as not supported.

Happy to help test any of these.

---

**Affected component:** channel
**Severity:** S2 - degraded behavior
**Version:** 0.8.5 (local/master-upgrade-2, post #11651 head)
**Workaround:** mention the bot in a fresh message (or reply to one of the bot's messages) instead of editing; edits are not observed at all.

| `runtime_profiles.<alias>.history_pruning.collapse_tool_results` | Inert | Declared + defaulted; no code path reads it. |

| `runtime_profiles.<alias>.history_pruning.enabled` / `.max_tokens` | Partial | Only lower the `effective_context_budget()` diagnostic threshold; they do not trigger trimming. |
| `runtime_profiles.<alias>.max_context_tokens` | Diagnostics only | Meter/floor warning, not a proactive trim trigger. |

References: `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/scattered_types.rs` (definitions), `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs` (`effective_context_budget`, ignored-warning collector), `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs:7569` (`keep_tool_context_turns` gate).

### Expected behavior

Pick one, per key:

- **Implement** the behavior the name/doc promises (preferred for `history_pruning.*` if token-budget compaction lands; see related issue), or
- **Deprecate and validate**: emit a config validation warning/error when a no-op key is set, and mark it deprecated in the generated config reference.

The goal is that setting a context/history knob either changes behavior or tells the user it does nothing. Silent no-ops on a cost-sensitive surface are surprising.

### Impact

Affected users: anyone tuning context to control provider usage. Consequence: config changes appear to have no effect, leading to misdiagnosis of usage/quota problems.

### ZeroClaw version
v0.8.5 (`cb2b20a9fe59004b7ef03e123942d31f29236d15`)

### Operating system
Ubuntu (systemd user service), aarch64

### Regression?
Unknown

### Pre-flight checks
- [x] I reproduced this on the latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.title: [Bug]: history_pruning.keep_recent and collapse_tool_results are dead config knobs (no readers since #8196)
issues.body:
## Summary

After #8196 removed the legacy history pruner/compressor in favour of whole-turn trimming, two fields of `HistoryPrunerConfig` lost their last runtime readers but survived in the config schema:

- `history_pruning.keep_recent`
- `history_pruning.collapse_tool_results`

## Evidence

`grep -rn 'keep_recent\|collapse_tool_results' crates/ src/` hits only the definition site:

- `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/scattered_types.rs` — the struct fields, their serde defaults, and the `Default` impl. Zero readers anywhere in the workspace (runtime, channels, gateway, tools, fuzz, benches).

The live trimming path (`history_trim::trim_to_recent_turns`, budget-derived) never consults either field, so setting them changes nothing while looking operative. We hit this in production: our contour set `keep_recent = 4` on the worker profile believing it bounded retained history, and only a code sweep showed it was inert.

## Suggested action

Same treatment `context_compression` got in the commit defaulting it to false with the `context_compression_unsupported` validation warning:

1. Emit a `collect_warnings` entry when `keep_recent`/`collapse_tool_results` are set to non-default values, saying the knobs have no runtime consumer; or
2. Remove the fields outright (configs that still set them keep parsing — unknown fields are ignored).

We run option 2 locally (one-commit removal, 1950 config tests green) and can open the PR, or switch to option 1 if the team prefers a deprecation warning first.

## Environment

- zeroclaw 0.8.7 (v0.8.7-179-ge15dd1268c), Windows 11 service + Linux
- Introduced: survived #8196 (a8da397032)

issues.title: [Feature]: Write-only WebUI credential management and scoped secret references
issues.body:
### Summary

Provide an operator-only credential catalog under Storage → Secrets: metadata-only listing, write-only creation/replacement, disable/delete actions, and controlled credential references for approved tasks. Draft PR #12402 covers write-only management for existing plugin TLS bindings. This issue tracks the broader catalog and scoped runtime references.

### Problem statement

Operators need to provision service credentials without pasting them into agent conversations, model prompts, session history, or skills. Existing encrypted configuration and masked secret fields provide useful building blocks, but configuring a credential is different from authorizing an agent/tool to use it.

An operator should be able to say “query the service using credential `monitoring-api`”; the model should handle a reference, while an authorized backend component supplies authentication.

The security objective is to let agents perform explicitly authorized operations without exposing passwords, API tokens, private keys, or other secret values to the model. The agent supplies an alias. A trusted consumer enforces the grant and applies authentication inside its execution boundary. With an external vault such as OpenBao, ZeroClaw persists the reference and grant metadata while the secret value remains in the vault and is fetched at use time. This reduces what can be recovered from the host's persistent storage or backups. A compromised running daemon, service identity, or unrestricted process with the same privileges may still be able to request secrets within that identity's vault policy.

### Proposed solution

**1. Administrative UI**

- List only identifier, type, configured/disabled state, permitted consumers/destinations, and appropriate lifecycle metadata.
- Create or replace a secret through a password/multiline draft field over the authenticated administrative API.
- Once saved, return only set/not-set state or a fixed mask. No reveal, copy, export, plaintext read endpoint, or value-length disclosure.
- Support explicit disable and delete, with dependency warnings and clear confirmation. Explain that deletion from ZeroClaw does not revoke a credential at its upstream service or erase existing backups.
- Keep the submitted draft transient; clear it after success, cancellation, and navigation. Do not persist it in browser storage, conversation state, analytics, or error reports.

**2. Controlled use by reference**

- Expose an identifier to the model, never a generic tool that returns the stored value.
- Resolve the reference within the existing trusted tool/connector execution boundary. Reuse applicable plugin secret-binding mechanisms rather than creating a second source of policy.
- Bind use to explicitly authorized agents/components and, where applicable, trusted destinations and operations. Possession of a reference must not grant permission.
- Preserve tool approvals, sandboxing, destination policy, and normal operation authorization. A chat instruction may request use but cannot create a credential grant.
- Re-evaluate current authorization and credential enabled/version state at use time; do not retain stale grants after disable, replacement, or permission revocation.
- Ensure authentication is not forwarded on cross-origin redirects or to model-selected arbitrary endpoints. Do not interpolate secret values into arbitrary shell text, URLs, or process command lines.

**3. Storage and API protections**

- Reuse the established SecretStore/key-source abstraction and an appropriate canonical storage owner; do not introduce custom cryptography or a parallel plaintext store.
- This feature must refuse secret writes if encrypted storage is unavailable/disabled; it must not silently inherit plaintext storage.
- List metadata without decrypting values. Credential value writes and lifecycle mutations remain operator-only, including authorization revalidation at commit time.
- Apply the established session/origin/CSRF protections, no-store responses, input bounds, and safe error handling.
- Audit actor, credential identifier, consumer, operation and outcome, never the value. Secret values must not enter prompts, memory, tool results, receipts, logs, telemetry, or traces.

### Example operator workflow

1. Open **Config → Storage → Secrets**, choose **Add credential**, and enter a reference name such as `MEU_GMAIL`. Choose the credential type and supply its value in the write-only form. For OAuth, complete the provider's consent flow with the requested scopes.
2. Bind that reference to an approved agent and connector, with explicit destinations and operations where applicable. For `MEU_GMAIL`, grant a Gmail connector read-only access to the authorized mailbox.
3. In chat, ask “Read my unread Gmail messages using `MEU_GMAIL`.” The model sends the reference and operation to the connector. The backend checks the current grant, uses OAuth to read the mailbox and returns the authorized results. Chat and tool output contain no OAuth tokens.
4. Return to Secrets to replace, disable, re-enable, or delete the credential. The list shows metadata and state. A disabled reference denies subsequent use.

| Credential type | What the operator provisions | Example request by reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TLS certificates and keys | PEM CA certificate, client certificate and private key, or a supported certificate file format such as CER/DER | “Check the inventory API using `INVENTORY_MTLS`.” The connector uses the configured TLS profile for the approved destination. |
| API token or key | A token in a write-only field | “List open findings using `SCANNER_API`.” The scanner connector authenticates to its configured origin. |
| Username and password | A credential record containing a username and write-only password | “Check the account status using `PORTAL_LOGIN`.” An approved connector performs authentication for the configured service. |
| TOTP | A write-only enrollment seed bound to an approved authentication flow | “Run the approved status check using `OPS_MFA`.” The connector generates the one-time code in the backend and supplies it only to that service's authentication flow. |
| OAuth | Consent for an approved connector and its requested scopes | “Read my unread Gmail messages using `MEU_GMAIL`.” The Gmail connector uses the mailbox's read-only grant. |
| Other connector-specific secrets | For example, an SSH private key bound to an approved SSH connector | “Check uptime on the approved host using `FLEET_SSH`.” The SSH connector authenticates within its existing host and operation policy. |

These examples describe the target behavior. Each credential type needs a compatible consumer with explicit policy. The identifier alone grants no access. Secrets, derived TOTP codes and authentication headers stay inside the trusted execution boundary.

### External secret providers

Under **Config → Storage → Secrets**, show each registered credential's source alongside its alias and configured/disabled state. Example sources are **Local encrypted storage**, **1Password**, and **OpenBao**. An operator can bind an existing external reference to an alias such as `SCANNER_API` without copying the secret into local storage. In chat, “List open findings using `SCANNER_API`” works through the same consumer and destination grants regardless of the source.

- **1Password.** Reuse ZeroClaw's existing `op://` reference integration. Show the provider and binding state, and let authenticated operators configure references such as `op://Operations/Scanner/token`. Use the existing backend integration and a least-privilege service identity.
- **OpenBao.** Propose a KV v2 backend with an operator-configured server profile and an explicit mount, path, and field, for example mount `kv`, path `integrations/scanner`, field `token`. Keep authentication server-side, verify TLS, and restrict the service identity to the required paths.
- **Additional providers.** The same backend interface could support Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Cloud Secret Manager, and other secret managers. Each adapter would use native provider authentication and least-privilege policies, with the same alias, binding state, and consumer authorization in ZeroClaw.
- List only references registered in ZeroClaw and their metadata. Keep external locators operator-only. Resolve values within the approved backend consumer and fail closed on denied or unavailable references. List operations must not fetch secret values.
- Start with binding and unbinding existing external secrets. Disabling or deleting a ZeroClaw binding affects local use. Rotation and deletion in the external vault remain under that provider's policies. Evaluate external write support separately.

References: [1Password secret references](https://www.1password.dev/cli/secret-references) and [OpenBao KV v2](https://openbao.org/docs/secrets/kv/kv-v2/).

### Credential usage grants and SSH-first rollout

Add **Usage permissions** under Secrets, with a credential-centered view and links from each consumer profile. One alias can have multiple independent grants. Each grant identifies the consumer type and instance, permitted agent where applicable, exact destination and compatible authentication slot. The backend enforces these grants alongside existing tool approvals and operation policy. Keep grants default-closed, check live authorization before each use, and audit alias, consumer, destination and outcome.

1. **SSH keys first.** Add an **SSH keys** tab with alias, source, configured state, public-key fingerprint when available, and authorized destinations. Support write-only private-key provisioning through local encryption or external references. An SSH grant binds host, port and remote user and requires verified server host keys. Resolve the key inside the SSH executor or its agent and keep it out of model context and command arguments. Preserve task-owned connection reuse, close on task termination and enforce an idle limit. Include credential/grant identity in connection reuse and make revocation effective before the next command on an existing connection. Test a key authorized on two hosts, refused on a third, then revoked for one while the other still works.
2. **HTTP and MCP.** Preserve existing HTTP aliases and exact HTTPS origin rules. Remote MCP grants bind the configured server instance, origin and authentication field. Local MCP delivery requires a separate explicit grant and a documented trusted process boundary because that process receives the value. Re-evaluate grants before reuse of any authenticated connection.
3. **Plugins and skills.** Reuse plugin TLS profiles for host-applied client identities. Any plugin access to a raw value requires an explicit capability and instance grant. Skills, SOPs and scheduled work can declare alias requirements and call authorized consumers. Their declarations confer no access. Arbitrary Bash or Python injection is outside the initial scope.

A grant authorizes authentication and does not authorize arbitrary operations. Keep provider identities and transport verification under operator control. Treat this as a proposed extension of #12408, with SSH as the first implementation slice, and seek maintainer feedback on ownership before expanding the runtime boundary.


### Non-goals / out of scope

- A general password manager with stored-value retrieval or export.
- A new master-key algorithm, universal vault replacement, automatic import of existing secrets, or a new MITM proxy.
- An unrestricted shell secret-injection tool.
- Claiming that encryption at rest or a write-only UI isolates secrets from a compromised daemon or unrestricted same-user shell. That requires a separately assessed execution/security boundary.
- Automatically migrating, revoking upstream credentials, or changing existing installations' behavior.

### Alternatives considered

- Continue provisioning through CLI/configuration: useful, but lacks the requested administrative workflow.
- Supply secrets through chat/skills: creates avoidable exposure and should not be the intended provisioning path.
- External secret managers: retain them as a possible backend direction rather than requiring every installation to run an additional service.

Related: #12001 (broader egress proxy and secret substitution), #8398 (plugin permissions/config/secrets model), #8556 (set/not-set secret UI), and #12142 (existing public discussion of daemon-state access). This proposal should complement their ownership and threat-model decisions, not duplicate or bypass them.

### Acceptance criteria

- Network responses and metadata listing never disclose saved values or lengths.
- Unauthorized, revoked, cross-agent and wrong-destination use is denied, including authorization changes between request admission and commit/use.
- Create/replace/disable/delete are covered through the real API and UI boundaries; duplicate identifiers, concurrent changes, missing key material and storage failure have explicit behavior.
- Regression tests verify no secret appears in model input, output, history, audit payloads or error responses.
- Existing consumers/configuration remain compatible. Stored ciphertext and metadata have one canonical owner; no new long-lived policy snapshot becomes authoritative.

### Architecture impact

Gateway administration, dashboard Storage UI, encrypted secret storage, and narrowly scoped tool/connector credential resolution. Reuse existing ownership, authentication and permission contracts. The administrative UI and runtime reference consumption can be separate PRs after the design is agreed.

Please advise which existing subsystem should own the catalog, whether reference consumption should be planned under #12001/#8398, and whether the eventual design crosses the RFC trigger for a material security-model change or a new subsystem. This issue does not assume that approval.

### Risk and rollback

Principal risks are credential disclosure, confused-deputy use, stale authorization, and a misleading isolation promise. Keep the capability opt-in and default closed, enforce grants server-side, document limits, and preserve encrypted-state backups. Disabling the new surface should leave existing credential consumers unchanged; any migration needs a separately reviewed rollback plan.

### Expected routing

Needs maintainer design assessment.

### Next decision surface

Discussion on this issue and the related security/plugin design trackers. Seek maintainer feedback on ownership and authorization for the remaining scope. Promote to an RFC if the substantive design requires it.

### Breaking change?

No intended breaking change.

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] Removed personal/sensitive data and deployment-specific details.
- [x] Used neutral, project-focused identifiers and examples.

### SSH key custody and transport lifetime

The operator registers a write-only OpenSSH key or an external reference and explicit host, port, and remote-user grants. For OpenBao, the daemon persists the encrypted reference, fetches the key under its narrowly scoped service identity, and passes it over stdin to an ephemeral OpenSSH agent. The helper does not create a private-key file or expose the value to the model, command arguments, or tool output. The signer socket is under a mode-0700 task directory owned by the service user, and agent forwarding is disabled. The broker requires strict server host-key verification.

Once OpenSSH creates its authenticated multiplex listener, the broker shuts down the signer and unlinks its socket before granting the first command. Later commands reuse the authenticated connection and recheck the current destination grant. A revoked grant blocks subsequent broker commands even if a transport already exists. The master itself is closed on task completion, cancellation, or idle expiry.

The service account and root remain trusted. A process with the same UID may reach the signing socket during authentication or the authenticated multiplex socket during the task. Per-destination grants are enforced by the broker. Host isolation and least-privilege vault policy bound the impact of same-UID compromise. This design does not claim a security boundary against a compromised daemon or unrestricted same-UID execution.

issues.title: RFC: Scoped use of operator-managed service credentials
issues.body:
### Which RFC trigger does this meet?

Security: a new security layer or material change to the security model.

### Problem

Operators need to authorize an agent to perform a task against a service without disclosing the underlying credential to the model, chat, skill text, or general-purpose tools. Provisioning a credential and authorizing its use are distinct actions. Feature issue #12373 describes the workflow. The catalog and cross-tool authorization contract need a project decision.

### Proposal

Define an opt-in operator-managed credential catalog and a scoped-use contract for trusted consumers. The operator can grant more than one supported consumer access to a credential, with an explicit destination and consumer-specific constraints. The agent handles a reference. A trusted adapter resolves and uses the material only after ordinary tool, principal, and sandbox policy checks. A reference alone is not authorization.

### Design sketch

- Metadata-only listing and write-only creation and replacement through authorized administrative surfaces. Support disable and delete, with redacted audit outcomes. Keep existing configured credentials compatible and avoid silently granting new consumers access.
- Credential types and consumer grants are separate. User/password destinations can use a protocol-qualified address with an optional port. The consumer owns canonicalization and protocol-specific endpoint matching. A syntactically valid catalog entry does not enable a protocol or a consumer.
- HTTP authentication must match the configured HTTPS origin. Redirect, authority and header handling must prevent credential forwarding outside the authorized destination. For SSH, bind use to the approved destination, login and host-key verification. Keep the signing socket private to a narrowly scoped task broker, with no agent forwarding or sandbox escape. Define the behavior of already-running operations when a grant is revoked.
- Local encrypted storage and opt-in external backends use the same grant semantics. With an external backend, keep raw payloads out of ZeroClaw persistent storage and avoid fallback to plaintext or a different backend on resolution failure. External service identity and permissions remain deployment configuration.
- A skill may name a reference but cannot resolve it directly. MCP and plugin consumers require explicit typed integrations, their own reviewed trust boundary and opt-in grants. Storing TOTP seeds or other types does not itself authorize use.
- Coordinate the credential classification and enforcement model with #6971 and #7142. Coordinate principal and delegated-task authority with proposed #12131. The scope here is service-secret use, independent of inbound credential renewal.

### Alternatives considered

Keep per-tool secret configuration only. This is simpler but duplicates provisioning and cannot express a shared operator-managed catalog. Exposing unrestricted secret reads to the model, a shell or a skill would make destination enforcement and redaction unreliable.

### Non-goals

Generic secret retrieval, implicit use of a credential by arbitrary MCPs, and unrestricted browser or shell login. This proposal does not choose an organization-wide secret provider.

### Risks and mitigations

Test authorization across tool, credential, principal, and destination boundaries, including denied redirects, alternate SSH destinations, cancellation, live revocation, rotation, and unavailable backends. Never log payloads, and make failure modes observable through redacted metadata. Document per-platform setup and when external backends can keep secret payloads off persistent host storage.

### Breaking change?

No proposed breaking change. Existing configurations retain their existing behavior. Introduce the new contract opt-in and document rollback by disabling the integration or revoking its grants.

### Decision and revisit surface

Decide this contract here before landing implementation under it. See feature request #12373 and existing implementation prototypes #12402 (plugin TLS UI), #12408 (catalog and permissions) and #12418 (scoped SSH). These prototypes preceded this formal proposal and do not establish acceptance or grant a runtime holding-crate exception. Please identify which slices may proceed under existing authority and which should wait for ratification.

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] Examples, payloads, and logs contain no deployment credentials or personal data.

Drafted with OpenAI Codex assistance at the request of the submitting account, @CastelloBrancoTecnologia. Proposed for discussion.

issues.title: perf(cron): agent cron jobs run outside any session-key scope, so they get no provider prompt-cache affinity
issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S3 - minor issue

### Current behavior

Agent cron jobs call `crate::agent::run` / `run_with_capabilities` from `run_agent_job_inner` (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/cron/scheduler.rs`) without entering `agent::loop_::scope_session_key`. The gateway (HTTP and WS), channel orchestrator, ACP and RPC turn paths all enter that scope; the cron path only derives a memory session key from `session_path` for cleanup on failure.

So `TOOL_LOOP_SESSION_KEY` is unset for every request a cron job makes, and anything keyed on it treats the run as "outside a conversation". In particular, with #11403 (Codex `prompt_cache_key` + `session-id`) a cron run's tool loop sends no affinity key. #11403's description already names this limit ("Turns that never enter a session-key scope (cron jobs, for one) still send no key").

### Expected behavior

A cron run's tool loop is one conversation: its requests should share one session key for the duration of the run, so prompt-cache affinity (and anything else scoped on the session key) applies within the run.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Build with #11403 applied; use the `openai_codex` provider on the default ChatGPT endpoint.
2. Create an agent cron job (isolated session) whose prompt needs several tool calls.
3. Let it run and inspect `cached_input_tokens` per request in the cost log, plus the `llm_request` prefix fingerprints from #10990 (`system_sha256`, `tools_sha256`).
4. Observe: the system prompt and tool list are byte-stable across the run, but follow-up requests get no cache hits. The same build gets high hit rates in gateway and channel conversations.

### Impact

Cost and latency only. Cron tool loops re-bill their full growing prefix on every request. On one install, one daily job's run was 10 requests and about 506K input tokens, almost all uncached.

### Logs / stack traces

```
One cron run, 10 requests, stable system/tools fingerprints. input_tokens / cached_input_tokens:
29557/0  32613/0  35190/0  38857/0  47033/0  58948/0  63795/0  64328/0  67684/0  67756/35968

Same install and build, follow-ups with >=90% of input cached:
gateway conversations 87%, Discord channel 70%, cron 0-10%
```

Possible approach (not prescriptive): wrap the `agent::run` call in `run_agent_job_inner` with `scope_session_key(Some(<per-run key>), …)`, using a key that is unique per run for `SessionTarget::Isolated` (for example derived from `run_session_id`) and the job's persistent session for a non-isolated target. Points to check: other readers of `TOOL_LOOP_SESSION_KEY` (cost attribution, `tools/shell.rs`, `agent/safety_net.rs`, delegate inheritance) would start seeing a key for cron runs; the key should follow `session_keys::sanitize_session_key` conventions and must not collide with a key a chat conversation could produce.

Related: #11403, #10990.

### ZeroClaw version

v0.9.0 (master 6c78ba59b plus #11403; the cron path is unchanged on master 87461d1ac)

### Rust version

1.97.1

### Operating system

Raspberry Pi OS (Debian-based, aarch64)

0.2.190

There is now a single config for enabling 64-bit time_t: libc_unstable_time64. This can be set unconditionally; it opts in to 64-bit time_t on the following platforms that use 32-bit by default:

  • 32-bit Linux-GNU
  • 32-bit Linux-uClibc
  • 32-bit Linux-musl. Note that setting this flag also enables some other changes that happend in musl v1.2.
  • 32-bit Windows-GNU
  • ESP-IDF (all targets with this environment are 32-bit)

Most other 32-bit platforms are either already using 64-bit time_t, or are considered legacy and will not be gaining support from their upstream maintainers.

You can enable this using RUSTFLAGS:

RUSTFLAGS='--cfg=libc_unstable_time64' cargo ...

Note that there may still be some changes to features gated by this config option, hence "unstable"

prs.title: fix(web): restore FieldForm local drafts after Discard all
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - `discardAll` already drops every shared draft, comment, and tombstone, which hides the unsaved-changes banner
  - `FieldForm` keeps a separate local `draft` / `comments` map seeded on reload, and its section Save reads that local map
  - After Discard all, the mounted inputs stayed dirty, so editing another field and clicking the section Save included the discarded values in the PATCH
  - `discardAll` bumps a `discardGeneration` that FieldForm uses to restore mounted fields immediately from the last loaded entries (and to clear local comments, field errors, and the Saved badge), then refresh those values from the server in the background. A failed `/api/config/list` therefore cannot leave discarded edits saveable. The background refresh does not set the form-level `loading` flag, so mounted `FieldRow`s stay in the DOM (no spinner flash). Save-all still does not bump this counter, so it will not rewind a just-saved form to stale list entries; the background refresh picks up values written by an earlier Save all
- **Scope boundary:** Does not change Save-all, per-section save, or `discardPaths` / `discardSection` (those already `reload()` after a successful save). `EntityEnabledToggle` still persists `<prefix>.enabled` itself; after a successful flip, FieldForm keeps the in-flight list request (so other fields can update and a section Save reload can still clear the spinner) and re-applies the saved pill if that GET started before the toggle
- **Blast radius:** Web config surfaces that use FieldForm under `ConfigDraftProvider` (Browser, Tools, channels, agents, …)
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #12288

### What this does, simply

The config dashboard has a global Discard all button and each section has its own Save. Discard all was only clearing the shared unsaved-changes store. The form on screen kept the typed values, so Save still thought those fields were dirty. Editing a different field and clicking Save could write back a value you had already discarded. This PR makes Discard all also restore the mounted form to the last saved values, while keeping an immediately saved Enable/Disable pill as-is.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface` = `web`
- **Setup / preconditions:** Running dashboard with a Browser (or similar) section. A disposable config such as:

```toml
[browser]
enabled = true
session_name = "discard-saved"
native_webdriver_url = "http://127.0.0.1:9515"
```

- **Steps to run:**
  1. Open Config → Browser
  2. Change Session Name to `discarded-edit`
  3. Click the global Discard all button and wait for its banner to disappear
  4. Confirm Session Name shows `discard-saved` and section Save is disabled
  5. Change Native Webdriver URL and click the Browser section Save
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Discard restores Session Name immediately without replacing the form with a spinner. The later Save PATCHes only the URL. If `/api/config/list` fails during Discard all, Session Name still returns to the last loaded value and section Save stays disabled. If the Enable/Disable pill is clicked successfully while that refresh is still pending, the pill keeps the newly saved state after the stale GET returns, and that same GET still updates other fields (and a section Save reload that started before the toggle finishes can still clear the spinner).
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** After Discard all, Session Name still shows `discarded-edit` and Save stays enabled. The later Save persists both the URL and `browser.session_name=discarded-edit`.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `Web Permission Tests` runs `npm run test:permissions`, which now ends with `jiti src/components/sections/FieldForm.discard.test.ts` after the existing enable-toggle tests.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No live daemon/UI session on this box. The tests mount the real `UnsavedChangesBanner` and `FieldForm` through `react-dom/client` in happy-dom and assert input values, Save disabled state, PATCH payloads, the failed-refresh path, and that the session-name input DOM node stays mounted across Discard all while `/api/config/list` is pending.
- **Commands run and tail output:** on head `84b89dfebe437e76125733b036a3accbac64c5cb`, in `web/`:
  ```
  $ ./node_modules/.bin/jiti src/components/sections/FieldForm.discard.test.ts
  ✔ Discard all restores mounted fields so a later section save excludes them
  ✔ Discard all after an edit and a persisted toggle keeps the toggle
  ✔ Discard all after a persisted toggle then an edit keeps the toggle
  ✔ unsaved edits stay until Discard all
  ✔ Discard all after Save all restores the saved values, not the earlier ones
  ✔ Discard all while the section loads keeps staged edits discarded (oldest-first)
  ✔ Discard all while the section loads keeps staged edits discarded (newest-first)
  ✔ Discard all clears local edits even when the refresh fails
  ✔ Discard all keeps mounted fields visible while the refresh is pending
  ✔ Discard all does not let a pending refresh overwrite a saved toggle
  ✔ A saved toggle keeps a pending Discard all refresh so earlier server values are not left stale
  ✔ A saved toggle does not leave a pending section Save refresh spinning
  ℹ tests 12  ℹ pass 12  ℹ fail 0
  $ ./node_modules/.bin/jiti src/components/sections/FieldForm.enableToggle.test.ts
  ℹ tests 2  ℹ pass 2  ℹ fail 0
  $ npx tsc -p tsconfig.app.json --noEmit
  # no diagnostics in FieldForm.tsx or FieldForm.discard.test.ts
  # (other pre-existing errors in SopCanvas/Dashboard/generated API types are unrelated)
  ```
  The two new tests fail on `52a54519` (session name stays `discard-saved`; the form remains a spinner after the cancelled Save reload is released) and pass on this head.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Nothing beyond the rendered DOM tests; no live dashboard session against a running daemon.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `Exact final-interface output`
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `84b89dfebe437e76125733b036a3accbac64c5cb`, `web` surface: `<ConfigDraftProvider><UnsavedChangesBanner /><FieldForm prefix="browser" /></ConfigDraftProvider>` mounted with `react-dom/client` in happy-dom, mocked `/api/config/list`, `/api/config/sections`, `/api/config` OPTIONS, and `PATCH /api/config`.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** `FieldForm.discard.test.ts` output above.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Editing `browser.session_name` then clicking Discard all restores the input to `discard-saved` immediately, keeps that same input DOM node mounted (no spinner), disables section Save, and leaves the banner gone (no PATCH). A later edit of `browser.native_webdriver_url` followed by Save sends only that URL. If `/api/config/list` returns 503 on Discard all, the discarded session name is still cleared, Save stays disabled, and a later URL edit + Save PATCHes only the URL. The same restore happens when Discard all follows or precedes a persisted enable toggle; the pill stays on the saved value and the later Save does not rewrite `browser.enabled` or the discarded name. If the operator disables the entity while Discard all's list refresh is still pending, that GET still applies (so other fields written earlier are restored) but the saved pill is kept: the next click sends `enabled=true` rather than repeating disabled. If a section Save reload started before that toggle PATCH finished, the form does not stay behind a spinner.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** No live daemon/UI session; the DOM tests cover the rendered Discard all + section Save path from #12288.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? (`No`)
- New external network calls? (`No`)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? (`No`)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? (`No`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? (`No`)
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation:

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? (`Yes`)
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? (`No`)
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? (`No`)
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users:

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <merge-sha>` and rebuild web assets.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** After Discard all on a config section, mounted fields stay at the discarded values and a later section Save persists them.

prs.title: fix(web): refresh config form after Save all
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (rebased onto `2450c1775`)
- **What changed and why:**
  - Refresh mounted field forms after Save all so their saved baseline matches the value returned by the gateway.
  - Keep rows mounted during that refresh to preserve focus, scroll position and row-local state.
  - Preserve edits and comments made while a save or baseline refresh is in flight and ignore stale reload responses.
  - Clear loading state when the latest refresh finishes, including overlapping group and global saves.
  - Invalidate coalesced in-flight `/api/config/list` GETs when a config PATCH succeeds, so a read started after the save cannot attach to a request that began before it and report pre-save state as the newest result.
  - Run the rendered regression test in the required web CI job.
- **Scope boundary:** Web dashboard configuration state, the dashboard's in-flight GET coalescer for the config listing, its regression test, and CI wiring; no API contract, config schema, or migration changes.
- **Blast radius:** The shared config draft provider, mounted configuration forms, and the dashboard's in-flight GET coalescer (shared by every dashboard caller). Each completed Save all triggers one existing config-list request per mounted form, and each successful `patchConfig` now drops a pending coalesced config-list GET.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #12021.

### What this does, simply

The Save all banner and each settings group keep related draft state. Save all persisted the shared draft and dismissed the banner, but the open group kept comparing its value with the old baseline, so it still looked dirty. The form now refreshes the saved value in the background, keeping its rows mounted while the request runs. Later edits use the refreshed baseline, and edits made during a pending save remain staged.

The refresh also exposed a smaller race: the dashboard coalesces identical in-flight GETs, so a config-list read started immediately after a save could join a request that began before the PATCH landed and install pre-save values as the new baseline. A successful `patchConfig` now invalidates the pending coalesced config-list GET, so the next read performs a fresh request.

## Testing (required)

Local verification and the current CI snapshot are summarized below.

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes — the same steps show the reported difference on `master` and this branch.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `web` dashboard.
- **Setup / preconditions:** Run ZeroClaw with the web dashboard available and a config gateway; open Config → Channels → Global settings.
- **Steps to run:** Toggle “Show Tool Calls” from its current value, click the banner’s “Save all”, and inspect the Channels group. Then toggle it again to verify the group compares against the newly saved value.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The banner reports “No unsaved changes”, the group Save button is disabled, and another change shows as unsaved. During the background refresh, the field remains mounted and focused.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** After the same Save all action, the group still shows “1 unsaved change” and its Save button remains highlighted until the page or daemon is reloaded.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The required `Web Permission Tests` job runs `cargo web check`, permission/catalog tests, `npm run test:config-draft-save-all` (added by this PR), context tests and SOP tests. The Rust jobs cover the untouched workspace. Hosted checks for head `7158230a8` all pass: 53 successful jobs and 5 skipped non-required jobs, including `Security`, `Web Permission Tests` and `CI Required Gate`.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No live-daemon or cross-browser smoke test; this PR’s regression test covers the form transition, focus, comment retention and stale-request behavior in Happy DOM.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  - On rebased head `fa7f70b75` (Node v26.10.0): `npm run test:config-draft-save-all` — `# pass 1`, `# fail 0`; `npm run test:permissions` — `# pass 5`, `# fail 0`.
  - Earlier on the pre-rebase head (Node v24.22.1): `npm test` — passed, including `Save all refreshes the saved baseline and preserves in-flight edits`; `npm run typecheck` — passed (`check:generated` and `tsc -b`); `npm run build` — passed (Vite reported the repository’s existing chunks over 500 kB); `git diff --check` — clean.
  - `git diff --check` on the rebased head — clean.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Before the change, reproduced the issue on master commit `5d4b18d33` with a mock gateway. On this branch, the integration test clicks the switch and Save all, then observes the rendered status and group Save state. It delays the post-save config-list request and verifies the switch remains the same focused DOM node while an edit matching the old baseline stays staged until the new baseline arrives. It also switches sections during a pending save, overlaps a group save with global Save all, verifies a comment typed during the delayed GET survives, and verifies a stale pre-save response cannot replace the fresh baseline or clear the staged edit. Delayed successful and failed PATCH requests verify the latest input survives.
- **Visual interface evidence:** Exact final-interface output from the React DOM renderer. The delayed-refresh regression verifies stable DOM identity and focus, preserved edits until the new baseline arrives, and no spinner after overlapping saves complete.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `7158230a8186fb205c38fe6885791fd60a7b0014`, surface `web`; `web/src/lib/configDraftSaveAll.test.ts`.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** The final React DOM displays “No unsaved changes”; the group Save button is disabled and the switch has `aria-checked="true"`. During the delayed config-list refresh, the original switch remains the rendered node and retains focus; an edit back to the old value remains visible and dirty after the new baseline arrives. During an overlapping group/global save, the latest shared reload clears the spinner. Section changes during a pending PATCH preserve the latest draft; a comment typed during the pending GET remains visible and is carried by the next PATCH; a stale pre-save response cannot overwrite the fresh baseline; delayed success and failure cases also verify the newest input remains staged, with the failure error visible. Assertions are in `web/src/lib/configDraftSaveAll.test.ts`.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Toggle “Show Tool Calls” → click “Save all” → the saved value becomes true and the banner/group are clean. Edit while the next save is pending → the latest value remains staged; on a failed save the dirty count and error remain visible for retry. A read issued after the save cannot reuse a pre-save config-list response.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Rust formatting, clippy and Rust tests were not run because this change modifies only the web dashboard. `npm run typecheck`/`npm run build` were not re-run on the rebased head because they require `cargo web check` to generate `web/src/lib/api-*.ts`; the required CI job runs `cargo web check`.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No.
- New external network calls? The dashboard still requests the existing config listing after Save all. This PR adds no endpoint or third-party service; the coalescer change only forces a fresh GET of the existing config listing after a config PATCH.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- Upgrade steps: N/A.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the eventual squash-merge commit with `git revert <merge-sha>`; no data migration or manual state repair is required.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** A field group remains dirty after a successful Save all, shows a loading spinner after overlapping saves, loses field focus or row-local state, drops an edit or comment made while a save or background refresh is pending, or installs a pre-save config listing as the new baseline after a successful save. The focused regression test covers these behaviors.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

N/A — this PR does not supersede another PR.

prs.title: fix(runtime): emit single SBPL backslash for home-dotfile regex
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - The macOS Seatbelt "home dotfiles for tool configs" rule was emitted as `regex #"^/Users/[^/]+/\\."`, so `sandbox-exec` never matched `~/.cargo`, `~/.nvm` and similar (#12137). The grant is now a literal `(allow file-read* (prefix "<HOME>/."))` built through the existing SBPL string-literal escaper, so the `/` boundary is fixed and quotes/backslashes in `HOME` cannot break the profile.
  - The grant is scoped to the current account's absolute `HOME` only. There is no `/Users/[^/]+` fallback, and no grant at all when `HOME` is unset or relative.
  - After the grant, `deny file-read*`/`file-write*` subpath rules close `~/.ssh`, `~/.gnupg`, `~/.aws`, `~/.config` (the home entries of `default_forbidden_paths()`) plus `~/.netrc` and `~/.git-credentials`. Seatbelt is last-match, so these stay closed.
  - `SeatbeltSandbox::with_roots` resolves `HOME` once and delegates to a private `with_roots_for_home`, so tests inject a synthetic home instead of mutating process-global `HOME`.
  - Configured forbidden hidden paths now reach this profile: the constructor keeps each configured spelling alongside its resolved target, and maps the configured name onto the resolved HOME when HOME itself is an alias. A later replacement of that hidden alias therefore stays denied, matching the fixed-name `.netrc` replacement behavior.
- **Scope boundary:** Does not change the workspace/tier root rules, the system path rules, or Linux sandboxes. User-configured `forbidden_paths` that intersect the home-dotfile grant are now enforced in this profile (configured location and resolved target). Other configured exclusions still apply through the existing policy layer.
- **Blast radius:** Shell/tool commands run under the macOS Seatbelt sandbox.
- **Linked issue(s):** Fixes #12137

### What this does, simply

On macOS, sandboxed tool commands were supposed to be able to read tool settings in hidden folders in your home directory (for example Cargo or Node version manager config), but a doubled backslash meant the rule never matched. This PR makes that rule work for your own home folder only and explicitly keeps the folders and files that commonly hold keys and saved passwords closed.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `Yes` (macOS only; the module is `cfg(target_os = "macos")`)
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` (sandboxed shell tool)
- **Setup / preconditions:** macOS with `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`
- **Steps to run:** `cargo test -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib security::seatbelt`
- **Expected on this branch (after):** `seatbelt_home_dotfile_allows_tools_and_denies_credentials` passes: the synthetic `.cargo/config.toml` is readable; `Documents/private.txt`, `.ssh/id_test`, `.aws/credentials`, `.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `.netrc` and `.git-credentials` are denied.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** `~/.cargo/config.toml` is denied inside the sandbox.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Format, Lint, and the aarch64-apple-darwin `cargo check` cover formatting and compilation. They do not run this module's tests.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No CI lane runs `cargo test` for the macOS-only Seatbelt module, so the native test below is not exercised by required CI.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  - The three new pure policy-string tests (`generate_policy_home_dotfile_grant_is_scoped_to_home_with_path_boundary`, `generate_policy_home_dotfile_grant_escapes_home_literal`, `generate_policy_without_absolute_home_omits_home_dotfile_grant`) were compiled standalone with the policy functions extracted from this head and run on Linux: `test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed`.
  - The exact profile generated by this head for a synthetic home `.../zc-sbx-probe/o"brien.smith` was run under `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -f profile.sb` on macOS 27.0.1 (arm64):
    ```
    .cargo/config.toml        rc=0  tool-ok

prs.title: feat(providers): adapt Anthropic and Bedrock to adaptive-thinking Claude models
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Anthropic's current Claude generations (Fable 5.1, Fable 5, Opus 4.7, 4.8, Opus 5, Sonnet 5) think adaptively: they reject the fixed thinking budget, and they reject a temperature other than 1 while thinking is active, which on these generations is the normal state. The Anthropic and Bedrock adapters now read the model generation from the alias `model` and pick the request shape from it, so a new release needs no code change. Earlier models keep the fixed budget and their temperature.
  - The thinking level maps to `output_config.effort` on those generations, sent together with `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. A configured temperature is dropped with a warning naming the value, and a warning fires when the output cap is still at the 4096 baseline, because reasoning now counts against it.
  - The streaming parser never read thinking blocks (a long-standing TODO), so streamed tool loops dropped the reasoning the model had signed. They are now captured as one record per block and replayed only within the tool round that produced them, which keeps every existing history-trim path valid under the preserved-thinking rule.
  - New optional `thinking_display` field on the `anthropic` slot (`omitted`, `summarized` or `updates`) so an operator can read the reasoning per provider entry; the runtime shows only the readable text, never the signed record. The generation matrix also carries a display axis: generation 5.1 and later accept only `summarized` and `omitted`, so a configured `updates` is sent to them as `summarized` with a warning naming the substitution (option (b) of #10617), whichever knob it came from.
- **Scope boundary:** No typed provider-refusal handling: that work is consolidated in #9272 and was removed from this branch (see "Relationship to #9272"). No global default changes for output caps or timeouts. No reasoning display on Bedrock. No doctor checks for these aliases. No quickstart auto-fill of `context_window`. No capture of `redacted_thinking` blocks. RPC sessions (zerocode) still send no thinking level, so they run at the model's default depth. No behavior change for temperature on the adaptive generations beyond the existing drop-with-warning; only the wording was narrowed.
- **Blast radius:** Every Anthropic and Bedrock alias (request shape changes only on adaptive-generation models), the config schema (one additive optional field), the runtime's reasoning display forwarding, and the display value sent for `agent.thinking.display = "updates"` on generation 5.1 and later (now `summarized`).
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #10617 (this PR implements its option (b) for both display knobs; closing it is the maintainer's call). Related #9272 (owns typed provider-refusal handling; see below).
- **Labels:** live snapshot: `enhancement`, `docs`, `core`, `agent`, `channel`, `config`, `gateway`, `provider`, `runtime`, `distinguished contributor`, `provider:reliable`, `provider:anthropic`, `channel:core`, `provider:bedrock`, `tool:delegate`, `needs-maintainer-review`, `risk:medium`, `size:XL`, `channel:acp`, `cli`.

## Relationship to #9272

This PR carries no refusal code. Commit `4dfc2b985e` removed everything this branch had added for declined requests, so there is one implementation of typed provider refusals to review and carry forward, and it lives in #9272. What went: `RefusalCategory`, `ProviderRefusal`, `is_provider_refusal` and `StreamError::Refusal` in `zeroclaw-api`; the refusal stop-reason parsing, the stop-details struct, the category classifier and the fallible `parse_native_response` shape in the Anthropic adapter; the whole refusal layer in `ReliableModelProvider`; the typed cause on `StreamErrorWithUsage`, the category message keys and the `Refused` render arm in the runtime; the seven refusal keys in all five `cli.ftl` catalogues; and the one docs sentence about classifier declines. `grep -ri refusal` over this PR's diff against `origin/master` returns nothing.

Until #9272 lands, a `stop_reason: "refusal"` is not special-cased: the response has no text and no tool calls, so it takes master's existing semantic-empty terminal path, which retries twice and then delivers the invalid-semantic-completion message. That is the behavior on `master` today, unchanged by this PR.

This PR keeps what it is for: adaptive request shaping, effort and display compatibility, and signed-thinking replay.

## Reconciliation with #10542

#10542 (merged, shipped in v0.8.5) landed the shared `ThinkingDisplay` wire enum, the optional `display` field on `NativeThinkingParams`, the beta header plumbing, and streamed thinking capture on the display path. This branch merges master and keeps all of it: the two adapters resolve one `display` value per request, the beta header `thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18` goes out whenever the request carries a display field (master's rule since #10542), and this PR's broader generation matrix and Bedrock work sit on top. The one behavior this PR adds on the shared path is the generation gate on `updates` described above.

## Precedence decision

Both display knobs stay. The order, highest first:

1. An explicit session-level display (the RPC `session/configure` control added by the stacked PR #10636).
2. `providers.models.anthropic.<alias>.thinking_display`, whenever it is set. `omitted` on the entry means the API default: no display field is sent, whatever the profile says.
3. `agent.thinking.display`, applied only when the entry leaves its knob unset.
4. The API default (no display field).

This is the same entry-overrides-profile pattern that `temperature` and `max_tokens` already follow. Before this revision an entry set to `omitted` mapped to no value and fell through to the profile's setting; an explicit entry value now always wins. #10636, which stacks on this branch, implements the session-level step at the top of that order and so reflects the same decision; it is refreshed on this head.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` and `tui` (zerocode)
- **Setup / preconditions:** An `[providers.models.anthropic.<alias>]` entry with `model = "claude-fable-5-1"`, `max_tokens = 32000`, `timeout_secs = 900`, `context_window = 1000000`, `thinking_display = "summarized"`, `fallback_models = ["claude-opus-5"]`; a second alias with `temperature = 0.2` and `max_tokens = 2048` as a negative control; a third on `claude-sonnet-4-5` with `native_thinking = true` in its runtime profile as a regression control; a fourth on `claude-fable-5-1` with `thinking_display = "updates"` as the display-fit control; a runtime profile with `[runtime_profiles.<alias>.thinking] default_level = "high"`.
- **Steps to run:**
  1. `zeroclaw --verbose --log-level debug agent -a <agent> -m "Use the shell tool to run ls, then summarize what you found."`
  2. Send the same with a `/think:max` prefix, then `/think:low`, then `/think:medium`.
  3. Run one turn on the negative-control alias with `-p anthropic.<bad-alias>`.
  4. Run one tool turn on the regression-control alias.
  5. Run one turn on the display-fit alias.
  6. In zerocode from this branch (`./target/release/zerocode`, so it spawns the sibling `zeroclaw`): pick the Fable alias from the title bar, run a tool task with the thought panel open, then switch to `claude-opus-5` from the title bar and send another message.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The `anthropic streaming provider request prepared` debug event reports `"thinking": "adaptive"`, `"effort": "high"`, `"stream": true`, no `budget_tokens` and no temperature; the second tool round succeeds. Step 2 changes the logged effort to `max`, `low`, then none. Step 3 logs `temperature dropped: this model generation only accepts temperature 1 while thinking is active` and `max_tokens is at the baseline; reasoning counts toward it on this model generation, so raise it on the provider entry`. Step 4 still sends `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: 10000}` with `temperature: 1.0`. Step 5 logs `thinking display fitted: this model generation accepts only summarized or omitted, so updates was sent as summarized` and the request succeeds with `display: "summarized"` on the wire. Step 6 shows prose in the thought panel, and the request after the model switch succeeds.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** With `native_thinking = true`, master (since #10542) sends `claude-fable-5-1` the adaptive shape with the temperature pinned to 1 and no `output_config.effort`, so `/think:` levels change only the prompt prefix and never the request depth; with it off, a configured temperature goes out unchanged and is rejected while thinking is active, and no thinking object is sent at all. Streamed tool loops replay no thinking blocks unless a display value is set. `agent.thinking.display = "updates"` on `claude-fable-5-1` returns 400 (`thinking.adaptive.display: Input should be 'summarized', 'omitted'`), and an entry-level `thinking_display` does not exist. The thought panel shows nothing or raw JSON records.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** The required `cargo nextest` workspace job covers the provider, api, config and runtime crates changed here; `Docs Style` (docs quality and links gates) covers the two changed Markdown files; the comment hygiene gate covers the Rust comments this branch adds.
- Hosted CI on this head (`d74778eb1396736869780c431995c56de43a2ac3`): `CI Required Gate` SUCCESS, run 34560876208. `Advisory Windows nextest (scoped, plugin-host=true)` failed (non-required; maintainers attribute it to an inherited CI-script problem, not this PR).
- **Historical hosted CI:** the previous exact-head run for `22d912be378a10b30b5d998e1da7d989e2d83a60` ([run 34164949852](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/34164949852)) reported `CI Required Gate` SUCCESS, along with `Test`, `Lint`, `Format`, `Security`, `Docs Style`, `MSRV (declared floor)` and the per-target `Check` jobs.
- **Advisory Windows nextest:** that run's non-required `Advisory Windows nextest (full, plugin-host=true)` job failed. Maintainers attribute this to an inherited CI-script failure (blank `--package` arguments and the `../../web/dist` packaging assertion) rather than to this PR; it is not claimed as passing here.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** No CI job calls the live Anthropic API, so the adaptive request shape, the streamed thinking capture, and the fitted `summarized` request on generation 5.1 are verified by unit tests and SSE fixtures rather than a real response. The 5.1 display boundary rests on one live probe of `claude-fable-5-1` (by the reviewer, 2026-09-04); `updates` was not probed on Opus 4.7, 4.8, Opus 5 or Sonnet 5. Whether Bedrock forwards `output_config` through `additionalModelRequestFields` is likewise unverified. The removal in `4dfc2b985e` carries no regression test of its own: a test for the post-removal `stop_reason: "refusal"` path would reintroduce the vocabulary the removal is meant to clear from this branch, and that path is master's existing semantic-empty terminal behavior, already covered by master's tests.
